desc:
Analyzing and designing public policies require a deep understanding of the behavior of economic agents such as consumers, producers, and the government. This course covers the standard microeconomic theory with applications to public policy analysis. Our goal is to show the nature of the market mechanism and its limitations (i.e., market failure) which justify some public policy interventions.

Course Goals:
Students are expected to acquire the skill sets of intermediate microeconomics including solving various optimization problems.

Course Contents:
The course will cover the following topics: (1) consumer behavior, (2) producer behavior, (3) market equilibrium, (4) market failure, and (5) an introduction to game theory and market design. See the Class Schedule Details.

Macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole, including growth in incomes, changes in prices, and the rate of unemployment. It attempts both to explain economic events and to devise policies to improve economic performance.

Course Goals:
The goal of this course is to understand both short-run topics, such as the business cycle, and long-run topics, such as economic growth and the effects of government debt. Also, it is to understand how both fiscal and monetary policies affect the economy as a whole.

The lecture will be given in English on economic analysis of tax policies, and more specifically, on basic tax theory and methods of empirical analyses, with some future empirical research projects in mind.

Course Goals:
Students will learn the basic theories of tax policy and understand the impact of various tax policies on the economic behavior of private agents. In addition, they will learn how to conduct empirical analysis on the effects of changes in tax systems on economic behavior. This knowledge will be useful when APPP students write their empirical master’s thesis, which is a requirement for completing the APPP program.

Course Contents:
This course covers basic theories and empirical methods of economic analyses of tax systems in a lecture format. The course will cover the followings: (1) Tax incidence, Tax distortions, Optimal taxation, and other issues; (2) Changes in the behaviors of economic agents caused by various tax changes, including personal income tax, corporate income tax, capital tax, and value added tax (or consumption tax).

We will follow the contents of Gruber’s textbook and solve the corresponding questions. In addition, we will read relevant academic papers to focus on empirical applications.
Please submit all assignments for the lecture preparation and review.

This course examines the composition elements and basic functions of tax system and tax administration through comparative study of those of the participants’ countries. The axis of comparison will be experience of Japan lectured in the classes. The participants will be required, as for their countries’ own tax system and administration, to learn how to search for ideal ones, find out inherent problems, and make the concept of solutions.

Course Goals:
(1) Understand the basic financial policy, tax system and administration of Japan and each participant’s country.
(2) Understand differences on the financial policy, tax systems and administration among the participants’ countries and deduced factors that bear them.
(3) Understand relationship between the Constitution and tax laws of each participant’s country.
(4) Understand the current problems and solutions for reaching to the ideal tax policy and administration of each participant’s country.

Course Contents:
The lecture (which consists of 13 classes) will cover the following topics:
<Class 1-2>
Overview of Japanese financial policy, tax system, and tax administration
<Class 3-6>
Comparative Study of financial policy, tax system and tax administration of the participants’ countries (Presentation and discussion by the participants will be required.)
<Class 7-10>
Comparative Study of the tax-related provisions in the Constitutions of the participants’ countries (Presentation and discussion by the participants will be required.)
<Class 11-13>
Consideration of the current problems and solutions for reaching to the ideal　 tax policy and administration of each participant’s country.
(Note) Some topics relevant to the above shall be picked up in the class.

This course examines the international tax system and tax policy through lectures based on Japan’s experience and discussions among participants. International taxation is a field of tax law and practice where many issues remain unsolved. We encourage proactive participation from all attendees.

Course Goals:
This course will equip students with the ability to discuss legal theories of the international tax system and to propose tax systems relevant to their own national context.

Course Contents:
The lecture will cover the following topics:
(1) An overview of fundamental issues of international taxation;
(2) A review of typical international tax systems, including Japan’s; and
(3) Policy discussions on designing a desirable international tax system.
Students will encounter and examine various unresolved issues in international taxation during the course.

In this course, the instructor gives academic-based notion and evidence of fiscal decentralization, including (i) function assignment between the central and local governments, (ii) normative functions of intergovernmental transfers to fill vertical and horizontal fiscal gaps and (iii) taxes suitable to local level governments so as to meet fiscal accountability at margin. (iv) Focus is on macroeconomic consequences of fiscal decentralization as well as microeconomic, i.e., allocative and distributive implications. specific issues to developing countries such as (v) management capacity of local governments, (vi) inadequacy of local government funding are also discussed. Not only country specific matters but also common challenges associated with decentralization will be addressed.

授業科目の到達目標:
The students understand theory and empirical evidence of fiscal decentralization. They should learn their country's experience on fiscal decentralization

授業の内容:
Part I: Overview of Fiscal Decentralization
・ Normative criterions on task allocation between the central and local governments.

Part II: Economic Theories of Decentralized Fiscal System.
・ Benefits of decentralization: (i) Decentralization Theorem, (ii) Tiebout mechanism(“Voting with feet”), (iii) Yard stick competition, (iv) Leviathan hypothesis, (v) Experimentation.
・ Costs of decentralization: (i) spillovers, (ii) tax competition, (iii) tax exporting, (iv) vertical tax externality
・ Macro economic consequences of decentralization; theory and practice
・ Criterions on good local taxes and their practices

Part III: Intergovernmental Relations
・ Normative implications for central polices in a decentralized fiscal system: (i) central regulation, (ii) intergovernmental transfers.
・ Positive views on central government regulations: (i) soft budgets, (ii)flypaper effect

The course is not for the public investments theories in general.
The course focuses on public private partnership for infrastructure instead of general theories on public investments.
The course primarily provides a guidance for students on the definitions, modalities, structures, procedures, contracts, financing, monitoring, and various implementation issues of public-private partnerships (PPPs) for public infrastructure, from the viewpoints of central or local governments who design them. It also discusses the specific conditions and limitations under which PPP works well and creates the value for money for the benefit of taxpayers.
The students are expected to understand at the completion of this course that PPP is not a panacea for fiscal problems of public sector, its success depends upon the careful designing of PPP projects by public entities, and specific measures to avoid the opportunistic behavior of private concessionaire.
Your proper understanding of PPPs will become clearer by your final reporting exercise of drafting an office memorandum on a specific project as the head of PPP department for the inter-governmental committee, which involves repeated comments back from the lecturer.

Course Goals:
[Objective]
This course aims primarily at acquiring practical knowledge on the public-private partnership for economic infrastructure. It covers all the relevant practical issues on PPP, starting with its origins and history and its background and economic reasoning, various definitions, distinction with privatization and various types and modalities and, also leading to issues on why it has become relevant for policymakers, its merits and demerits, conditions under which PPP works well, sectors and projects suitable or not suitable for PPP, the most difficult part of designing effectively PPP, appropriate risk allocation, substantial renegotiation of PPP contracts, recent criticism on PPP, how to select the best concessionaire and so on. The course of course will take a look at various concrete examples of PPP projects, successful or unsuccessful ones to discuss the issues.
The other important objective of this course is to learn the basic economic theories on PPP. Actually, most of the important economic theories on PPP are all literally covered by the book of Engel et al (2014). We will go through them to the extent possible so that we will be able to explain the PPP issues also in the context of economic theories. Surprisingly, PPP is one of the major topics which great economists like Jean Tirole and Oliver Hart were willing to pick up as the theme of their papers.

Expected Results
After having successfully completed this class, the students are expected to understand the precise concept of PPP both on the basis of (1) practices and realities and (2) insightful economic theories. Just for example, according to widely shared popular views, it is often noted that PPP can be effectively introduced in reducing the constraints on public debt and annual budgets of the governments and local states which face the scarcity of revenues in comparison with mounting pressures for social spending. Another popular view is that PPP can effectively transfer most project risks to the private party at a competitive pricing minimized by the transparent tendering process. But the reality is different. The course is expected to enable the officials of public sector to adequately recognize the effectiveness and limitations of PPP and to design PPP effectively.

This course provides theoretical and practical analyses of industrial organization, game theory, economic regulation, and public enterprises. Through lectures and class discussions, students will examine both classical and contemporary issues in business economics and public policy.
Classical topics include economic regulation and ownership structures in public utility industries such as power, telecommunications, and transportation. Contemporary topics include consumer marketing analysis, causal inference, innovation, and platform economics. The course also introduces research methodologies using large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI).
Empirical studies will be examined to illustrate key theoretical and policy issues. Research presentations by participants are required.

Course Goals:
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
1.Understand the theoretical foundations of industrial organization and economic regulation.
2.Analyze ownership structures and regulatory frameworks in public utility industries.
3.Apply quantitative methods to economic analysis in industrial organization and business economics.
4.Evaluate contemporary issues such as platform economics and innovation using modern analytical tools, including LLMs.
5.Present research findings clearly and professionally in the fields of economic regulation and business economics.

Lectures will be given on basic theories and methods of empirical analysis for research on social security systems, with a view to future empirical/theoretical research.

Course Goals:
This lecture will cover basic theories of social security systems and impacts of various social security policies on behaviors of private economic agents. It will also provide students with a foundation for conducting empirical analyses of the impact of changes in the social security system on economic behaviors.

Course Contents:
Course Contents

This lecture will cover key theories and empirical methods used in the economic analysis of social security systems. We will study 1) social security systems, 2) employment and workers' compensation insurances, 3) health and medical insurances, and 4) welfare policies, and examine possible changes that these policies bring about in the behaviors of private economic agents. The lecture will proceed by introducing actual systems in Japan and the United States. Ultimately, students are expected to engage in their studies with a view to empirical analysis of social security systems in their home countries.

Outline of lectures

１． Introduction
After explaining the lecture's objectives, positioning, contents, method of proceeding, and grading method, I will introduce various types of social insurance (pension and social security systems, unemployment and workers' accident compensation insurance, health and medical insurance, welfare policies such as livelihood security, etc.), and will list topics to be covered in the subsequent lectures.

２．Social insurance
As a start of our economic analysis of social security policies, we will study why people value social insurances and why it is not adequately provided in a competitive market. The course will also introduce the concept of moral hazard that can arise when there are social insurances.

３．Social Security
This lecture will cover social security and pension systems that guarantee the life after retirement and examine the impact of their presence on consumption smoothing over the lifecycle. The impact of the presence of social security and pensions on the labor supply of the elderly will be discussed. The sustainability of the social security and pension systems and possible reforms of the systems will also be discussed.

4． Unemployment Insurance and Workers' Compensation
Unemployment insurance and workers' compensation insurance will be studied to provide an overview of the systems and how their presence affects consumption smoothing and people's willingness to supply labor.

5． Unemployment Insurance and Workers' Compensation (cont.)
We will empirically investigate how unemployment insurance and workers' compensation insurance affect the behaviors of private economic agents and discuss the design of more desirable unemployment and workers' compensation insurances.

6．How to find a topic for a research paper
Keeping the fact that students are required to submit an empirical term paper at the end of the semester in mind, this lecture provides tips for writing empirical papers in the field of economics. Based on my own experience as an empirical economist, I will try to give you advice on how to find a good paper topic and how to structure an easy-to-understand paper.

7．Health Insurance
This lecture will provide an overview of medical and health insurance systems for health risks, and examine how their presence affects consumption smoothing, people's attitudes toward health care, and the behavior (choice) of health care service providers. In addition, we will empirically study how medical and health insurances affect the behaviors of private economic agents and discuss the design of more desirable medical and health insurances

8．Income Distribution and Welfare Programs
After reviewing some indicators that capture income distributions, this lecture will study various social welfare policies through income redistribution and examine how their presence affects people's attitudes toward economic behaviors, especially the labor supply. We will empirically examine how the social welfare policies affect behaviors of private economic agents and discuss the design of more desirable social welfare policies.

9． Presentation
Students will be asked to present proposals for the empirical analysis on their own country's social security system (20 minutes per student). Though it is not necessary to have a completed result of your empirical analysis, I would like you to make an easy-to-understand presentation on an interesting topic in accordance with the social security theories and methods of empirical analysis you have learned in this course.

１0． Presentation (cont.)
Continuing from Lecture 9, students will be asked to present some papers related with your proposals for empirical analyses using their own country's social security system.

１1． Presentation (cont.)
Continuing from Lecture 9, students will be asked to present some papers related with your proposals for empirical analyses using their own country's social security system.

１2． Presentation (cont.)
Continuing from Lecture 9, students will be asked to present their preliminary results based on empirical analyses using their own country's social security system.

This course examines how public institutions—particularly central banks and deposit insurance systems—design and implement frameworks to ensure financial stability. Drawing on Japan’s historical experience with asset bubbles, bank failures, and systemic risk, the course provides conceptual and policy foundations for understanding risk governance. Students will engage with key institutional roles, regulatory tools, and crisis response mechanisms through case studies and discussion. The course is especially suited for those interested in policy design under uncertainty and institutional resilience.

Course Goals:
• To understand the conceptual differences between crisis management and risk management.
• To evaluate how central banks and deposit insurance systems contribute to financial stability.
• To analyze real-world cases of bank failures and government interventions in Japan.
• To simulate the role of policymakers in managing financial crises.

Course Contents:
This course is structured over 13 sessions, each lasting 105 minutes, and is designed to progressively build students’ understanding of financial stability, risk governance, and institutional design in the context of Japan’s policy experience. The first part of the course introduces key concepts and distinguishes between risk management and crisis management in public sector contexts. Students will examine real-world examples of systemic shocks—such as the collapse of Long-Term Credit Bank (LTCB) and Hokkaido Takushoku Bank—and trace the policy and institutional evolution that followed.
In the middle sessions, students will study the institutional roles of the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and the Deposit Insurance Corporation of Japan (DICJ), including their mandates, supervisory mechanisms, and their coordinated responses to systemic risks. Detailed attention will be paid to micro- and macroprudential regulatory approaches, on-site and off-site monitoring practices, the Lender of Last Resort (LOLR) function, and moral hazard considerations in the design of safety nets.
In the final third of the course, students will apply their accumulated knowledge through a structured policy simulation, role-playing decision makers responding to a hypothetical financial crisis. This exercise is designed to enhance analytical thinking, teamwork, and the capacity to propose context-sensitive policy solutions. The course concludes with student presentations, peer feedback, and a synthesis discussion to reflect on lessons learned and their applicability to participants’ home countries.
To support their learning, students are expected to complete assigned readings before each session, review policy documents related to their own country’s financial institutions and safety net structures, and actively participate in class discussions. Periodic reflection assignments will be used to reinforce learning and encourage comparative analysis.

This course covers international trade, international finance and investment. The emphases are put on understanding of the current international economic and financial policies as well as the international organizations and their rules (WTO/GATT, IMF, AMRO, etc.).

The course is divided into three parts. In the first part, we cover international trade theories, policies, and related international organizations (e.g., WTO). In the second part, we study international finance theories, policies, and related international organizations (e.g., IMF, ESM, AMRO, and others). The third part focuses on theories and policies related to cross-border investments, which have become increasingly important for emerging markets. Additionally, we discuss current issues in international economics, such as the financial crisis.

Course Goals:
The goals of this course is as follows:
(1) deeper understanding of Macroeconomics
(2) understanding of international trade and finance theories that are relevant to the policy making for the emerging economies
(3) understanding of current policy issues (e.g. bilateral trade frictions, developments of the Global Financial Safety Nets, external debt management)
(4) understanding of the international fora's roles in this field (such as G20, ASEAN+3 (China, Japan and Korea) and related international organizations (such as WTO, IMF, AMRO)
(5) understanding of the function that cross border investment plays for the emerging market economies and potential risks related to it

(8) Global financial crisis

We study basic theories and empirical methods to conduct economic analysis of the public sector. In addition, we discuss specific policies of Japan, the U.S., and Asian countries.

Course Goals:
Together with "Economics of the Public Sector II" in the spring/summer semester, students will learn the must-know basic theories and empirical tools for economic analysis of the public sector.

Course Contents:
Contents

Lectures will cover (1) basic theories of public economics, (2) empirical methodologies widely used in public sector economic analysis, and (3) examples of public policy analysis in Japan, the U.S., and other Asian countries. In addition to learning the contents of the lectures, students are expected to be aware of how the content learned in the lectures can be applied to analysis of policy issues facing their own countries.

Outline of each lecture

１．Introduction & Defining Public Sector Responsibilities
After explaining the objectives, position, content, method of proceeding, and grading procedures of this course, we will examine the core question of public economics, namely, when public sector intervention is justified in a mixed economy.

２．Measuring Public Sector Size
After considering definitions of government and the public sector, we will review the roles played by government and the public sector in a mixed economy (production of public goods, regulation, taxation, subsidies, purchase of goods, and redistribution). We will also consider several indicators of the scale of government and public sector activity.

３．Theoretical Tools of Public Economics I
The course will review basic mathematics that is the minimum foundation for studying public economics and the problem of maximizing the objective function under constrained conditions, using the case of subsidies to single-mother households as a case study.

４．Theoretical Tools of Public Economics II
The basic theories used in the study of public economics will be reviewed, including the derivation of demand and supply functions, elasticities, market equilibrium, consumer surplus, producer surplus, social surplus, and the fundamental theorem of welfare economics (that under certain conditions, competitive market equilibrium leads to optimal allocation of resources).

５．Empirical Tools of Public Economics I
After learning the difference between correlation and causation, and randomized controlled experiments to identify causal relationships, students will learn what causal inferences can (and cannot) be made using time series and cross-sectional data available in situations where experiments cannot be performed.

６．Empirical Tools of Public Economics II
The methods of quasi-experiments (natural experiments) and difference-in-differences estimation will be introduced as a method of causal identification beyond time series and cross-sectional data. The advantages and disadvantages of reduced-form regressions and structural estimation will also be briefly explained.

７．Midterm Exam
A mid-term exam will be given during the first hour of the lecture. After the exam, an explanation of the questions will be given in class.

８．Market efficiency & Market failure
Examine the conditions under which competitive markets lead to efficient resource allocation and learn what market failures occur when these conditions are not met.

９．Public Goods
Students will learn about public goods as one factor that causes market failures. After defining public goods, we will confirm that public goods are not properly supplied in competitive markets and learn what role the government/public sector can play in solving this problem.

10　Externalities I
Learn about externalities as another source of market failures. After defining externalities, we will review what types of market failures occur in competitive markets with externalities. Negative and positive external economies will be examined with specific examples.

11．Externalities II
How to resolve the distortions in resource allocation resulting from externalities will be discussed, both in terms of private solutions and solutions through government and public sector intervention.

12. 　Environmental Externalities
As an example of the externalities, environmental problems will be discussed. We will learn that the optimal intervention depends on the type of environmental problems.

We study basic theories and empirical methods to conduct economic analysis of the public sector. In addition, we discuss specific policies of Japan, the U.S., and Asian countries.

Course Goals:
Together with "Economics of the Public Sector I" in the fall/winter semester, students learn the must-know basic theories and empirical tools for economic analysis of the public sector.

Course Contents:
We cover (1) basic theories of public economics, (2) empirical methods widely used in public sector economic analysis, and (3) examples of public policy analysis in Japan, the U.S., and other Asian countries. Students are expected to be aware of how the content learned in the lectures can be applied to analysis of policy issues facing their own countries.

Rough outline of each lecture (tentative and subject to change):
1. Introduction and Budget Analysis (I)
I explain the goals and positioning of the lectures, its contents, how to proceed, and the grading policy. Then, I provide an overview of the government's budget system to examine the public sector from a macro economic perspective. After studying the composition of expenditures and revenues, we discuss the meaning and limitations of various measures of the scale of public sector activities.

2. Budget Analysis (II)
We study the macroeconomic consequences of increasing budget deficits. In addition, we cover recent papers on fiscal stress.

3. Cost-Benefit Analysis
We study cost-benefit analysis, which is useful in determining the adoption of public projects. We introduce the types of costs and benefits that are not easy to measure, such as the value of time and human lives. We also cover the concept of discounted present value to make costs and benefits comparable between different points in time, and cost-effectiveness analysis when benefit evaluation cannot be done properly.

4. Political Economy (I)
We study the political process by which the adoption or rejection of public policy is determined. First, we cover the conditions for selecting policies of optimal size for the case where the government can appropriately aggregate the preferences of its constituents. Next, our focus is on examining the conditions under which the government can appropriately aggregate the preferences of its members in a society with a large number of members.

5. Political economy (II)
This lecture examines how a majority voting leads to a choice in the provision of public policy when the conditions for appropriate aggregation derived in the previous lecture are satisfied for direct and indirect democracies. We also study government failures that occur when the government serves its own interests rather than the interests of its members.

6. Mid-term Exam
A mid-term exam will be given.

7. Economics of Local Government (I)
We study fiscal federalism, or how to divide the roles of government into two parts: central government and local government. We introduce Tiebout model as a basis for considering the optimal division of roles among the governments.

8. Economics of Local Government (II)
Based on the Tiebout model introduced in the previous lecture, we study redistribution policies among regional governments. We consider when redistribution is necessary. We also examine the conditions under which grant policies are appropriate for redistribution. As an example of redistributive policies, we focus on the case of school finance equalization policy in the United States.

9. Education
In order to understand the public sector intervention in education, we examine the logic in which public intervention is justified. Next, we study the relationship between public expenditures on education and productivity of educational sectors. We also see the impact of education vouchers on educational outcomes.

10. National Defense
We overview how defense spending has changed over years, how it differs among nations, and how it relates to their historical background. Next, we examine how to determine the optimal level of defense spending. Some ideas on how to improve the efficiency of defense spending also will be examined.

11. Social Insurance
In order to understand the role of the public sector in the social insurance, we outline the reasons why government intervention in the social insurance market is justified. We also study the benefits and moral hazard costs of social insurance, and present examples of empirical analysis of the impact of social insurance on people's behaviors.

12. Welfare Policy (I)
We study welfare policy or redistribution policy. We discuss income distribution and indicators of social inequality, and then discuss the factors that determine the moral hazard costs of welfare policy (redistribution policy).

13. Welfare Policy (II)
We study how to design welfare policies to minimize moral hazard costs. We also review the conditions under which government intervention in a market economy is justified. We wrap up the lectures.

Sustainable Finance and ESG Investing

Overview.
Green and sustainable finance can play a key role in achieving one of the main goals of the Paris Accord, namely, “making finance flows consistent with a pathway towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development”.” The course will provide a brief overview of the major issues in sustainable finance and ESG investing. One of the main texts will be a report by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS, April 2022) entitled “Enhancing Market transparency to Scale Up Green and Transition Finance” (in bold font, below). The report covers taxonomies, green external review and assessment, and climate transition metrics and frameworks as well as sustainable finance and market products.

Course Goals:
Course Goals
1. To provide students with basic knowledge of the key concepts of green finance, or finance with the purpose of environmental objectives.
2. To train students to differentiate between various forms of financial instruments with sustainability labels, to provide students with knowledge of what current disclosure regimes are currently prominent and might emerge going forward, what are they key institutions of green certification and verification to ensure that promised benefits are achieved.
3. To provide students with knowledge of how taxonomies and green classification frameworks differ across jurisdictions and how they can be made interoperable; how future green rating system might be best designed.
4. To provide students with knowledge of what new technologies have the promise to boost ease of data collection and market transparency.
5. To provide students with regional expertise on the challenges specific to mainland China, Japan and Asia more generally.

Learning Outcomes.
1. Students should be able to describe and explain the creation and verification of green securities
2. Students should become able to use relevant information for making a decision about the alignment of investment opportunities with sustainability objectives.
3. Students should be able to demonstrate effective communications skiils in describing the pluses and minuses of various forms and instruments of green finance

Course Contents:
Class 1 (April 13)
Overview of Issues in sustainable finance.
Green finance is motivated by global climate goals. The course will provide a overview of the motivation for climate finance from the recent IPCC report, the explosive growth of green financial markets, documenting which type of issuers (sovereign, supranational, corporate) emerged first in bonds and in which jurisdictions. It will also review ESG in equity markets, as well as green investment mandates.

Class 2 (April 20)
Green and Transition Taxonomies.
What does it mean to be green? Different national regimes, and even different institutions or regions within nations can have different definitions of what it means to be green. To promote green financial markets, these taxonomies must have integrity. The European Union has made efforts to increase harmonization within member states, and emerging markets are looking to the EU model as a template. Beyond the EU, however, jurisdictional differences persist globally, reflecting divergent development priorities, as well as distinct jurisdictional properties. The EU-China initiative to improve the consistency of definitions and methodologies for determining eligibility of green projects—a “common-ground” taxonomy—that represents one of the most significant global efforts to date.

Class 3 (April 27)
Disclosure regimes and measurement.
Investors and financial intermediaries must be able to identify tangible physical outcomes and climate-related benefits from firm and country-level activity. Indeed, global initiatives such as the FSB’s Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures aim to make better environmental information readily available. The unit will review the changing disclosure environment and the reliability and quality of the key carbon emissions disclosure items.

Class 4 (May 11) .
Institutions of green certification and verification (4)
For investment in green securities to materially affect climate objectives, their environmental or climate-related benefits must be verifiable. This class will review the various type of institutions of certification available to investors and issuers These can includes approved external verifications, as well as green bond and stock indices that identify specific financial assets as green via a stated methodology. A limitation of indices is their binary nature: a financial asset is either green or it is not. Some providers have arisen that make more granular assessments. This unit will examine the attributes of various well-known certifiers.

Class 5, 1st half (May 18)
New green technologies: data collection and beyond.
This unit will focus on the new technologies’ promise to boost ease of data collection and market transparency in green finance. For example, technological advances in measuring carbon emissions in real time—utilising the so-called “internet of things”—will reduce data collection costs and increase data availability. The lecture will review examples of real-time verification of compliance with carbon emissions targets that are currently under development in Hong Kong (BIS Innovation Hub, 2021).

Class 5, 2nd half (May 18)
Trends in innovative financial instruments: SLBs and ESG, Transition Finance Metrics and Frameworks.
In this unit we provide an overview of green financial instruments, distinguishing the many various forms, emphasizing their key defining characteristics. Instruments can be equity versus debt, bank loans versus bonds, and can have payoffs contingent on varying outcomes at the project, firm or country level. Some shortcomings of existing labels related to ESG will be reviewed. We also will discuss how future green ratings systems might be best designed to align the incentives of firms, investors and other stakeholders, depending on the institutional setting, rated instruments and entities, and system objectives.

Class 6 (May 25)
The Experience in Emerging Asia (including China) and Japan
Asia both suffers most the consequences of climate change and will be the largest emitter of greenhouse gases going forward. Its experience will be of critical importance to the global combat to mitigate climate change. As for China, it has been a leader among emerging markets in both unifying its own regulatory framework to classify green finance activities and work towards achieving common ground in these classifications with the European Union. The features of the rapid growth of green financial markets in China will be reviewed and assessed.

Class 7 (June 1)
Final examination.

This course covers the policy issues regarding the regional financial arrangements and economic surveillance exercises in East Asia.

The Asian Financial Crisis of 1997-98 and the Global Financial Crisis of 2008-09 made the East Asian authorities (Ministries of Finance and Central Banks) to create a regional framework (CMIM/AMRO) to prevent and resolve currency crises in addition to the global framework of IMF. The authorities have come to recognize the importance of objective third party's view of economic and financial developments in order to be accountable to their own taxpayers, which led to conclusion of CMIM (multilateralized currency swap arrangement) in 2010 and establishment of ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) in 2011 and its transformation into an international organization in 2016. The ongoing developments to date will be covered.

Course Goals:
This area has not been covered by regular textbooks and become increasingly important for policy makers of emerging economies. The course aims students to acquire the following knowledge and skills:
(1) To understand the current international financial policies in East Asia,
(2) To recognize the challenges the policy makers face and how to overcome them,
(3) To master the practical knowledge and skills of international negotiation in East Asia, and
(4) To provide materials to consider the future of rule-based multilateral system under the present geopolitical context.

This course may also help students to gain practical knowledge about working at international institutions.

Course Contents:
(1) the developments of the regional financial arrangements in East Asia (such as CMIM or AMRO) since the Asian Financial Crisis of 1997-98,
(2) the developments and policies relating to cross-border capital flows,
(3) case studies of economic surveillance reports, financial surveillance reports and publication policy,
(4) the components of global financial safety net (IMF, regional financial arrangements (such as EFSF/ESM in Euro area, FLAR in Latin America, EFSD in former CIS countries, and CRA for BRICS countries in addition to CMIM/AMRO in East Asia), bilateral swap arrangements (such as US Fed's and China's PBOC's) and their own international reserves),
(5) the most current issues such as the global safety net’s reaction to the Covid-19, or the recent US policy toward the possible transformation of the international monetary system, and
(6) Next potential financial crises (by a guest speaker).

This course will introduce participants to the process of formulating a hypothetical macroeconomic and structural adjustment program, which assists them to gain basic skills in managing economic performance of any country. Thus, participants will be exposed to basic concepts of macroeconomic behavioral and accounting relationships that form a sound basis for analyzing economic developments and formulating economic policies.

Course Goals:
During the course, participants will acquire basic and practical skills that are useful in economic analysis and policy formulation. (Completion of macroeconomic and microeconomic principles at the APPP is prerequisite.)

Course Contents:
The participants will be divided into several groups, depending on the number of the participants in the class. Each group is likely to comprise 4 – 5 people and will be asked to produce two scenarios.

The first scenario is to forecast the economy of Sri Lanka in 1991, based on the assumption that there will be no change in economic policy beyond what is known at the end of 1990. This scenario is usually called as a “baseline” scenario. The forecast will cover the following accounts: the national income and prices, balance of payments, fiscal, and monetary accounts. In addition, the flow of funds table, linking these accounts, will need to be completed.

Once the baseline scenario is completed, the participants are expected to identify economic problems that Sri Lanka will be facing in 1991 and identify the need for improvement.

The second scenario, often referred to as an adjustment scenario, is to forecast the economy in 1991, based on the assumption that the authorities will introduce a set of policies, in order to improve economic performance relative to the baseline scenario.

For the adjustment scenario, the participants are to set targets for major economic variables, such as growth, inflation, or balance of payments and choose policy instruments, such as monetary or fiscal instruments, and are expected to explain how their choice of instruments are to help achieve the targets.

At the end of the workshop, each member of the group is expected to participate in presenting the result. Questions, answers, and discussion will follow the presentation.

This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the key principles, practices, and challenges in corporate finance. The module also equips students to analyze financing methods such as venture capital, Initial Public Offerings (IPOs), and debt policies, along with their associated costs and benefits. It emphasizes the dynamics of financial decision-making under conditions of asymmetric information, including its implications for capital structure, payout strategies, mergers and acquisitions, and the trade-offs in managing financial risk, taxes, and shareholder value. Students will develop critical insights into corporate governance mechanisms, the role of financial markets, and the importance of balancing shareholder and stakeholder interests in fostering responsible business practices. Students can acquire not only knowledge but also perspectives with global mindset and social responsibility through this course.

Course Goals:
This course aims to develop students’ understanding of how firms make financing and financial policy decisions. It introduces the fundamental sources of corporate financing, including equity and debt, and examines how financial markets and intermediaries support corporate funding. Students will learn how firms raise capital, evaluate alternative financing choices, and understand the economic trade-offs underlying capital structure decisions.

The course also explores key corporate policies and strategic decisions, including payout policy, mergers and acquisitions, and venture capital financing. In addition, it examines governance and incentive issues arising from agency conflicts, as well as broader perspectives on stakeholder capitalism and responsible business. By the end of the course, students should be able to analyse corporate financial decisions and understand how financing choices relate to firm value, incentives, and organisational objectives.

Course Contents:
Tentative topics:
1. Corporate Financing Fundamentals:
• Understand the key components of corporate financing, including shareholder equity, voting procedures, and major classes of securities.
• Examine the role of financial systems, markets, and intermediaries in corporate financing.
2. Venture Capital and Equity Financing:
• Analyse the role of venture capital and the processes and costs involved in Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) and private placements.
• Evaluate the costs and benefits of different methods of raising equity.
3. Debt Policy and Theories of Capital Structure:
• Explore the MM propositions on debt irrelevance and the trade-off between tax shields and financial distress costs.
• Critically assess the pecking order theory and its implications for financing decisions.
4. Payout Policy:
• Investigate the impact of dividends and share repurchases on shareholder value.
• Examine the relationship between taxes, payout policies, and the life cycle of firms.
5. Mergers and Acquisitions:
• Identify the types and motivations behind mergers and acquisitions.
• Assess the potential gains, costs, and implications of takeovers and corporate control.
6. Agency Problems and Corporate Governance:
• Analyse the agency problems arising from the separation of ownership and management.
• Evaluate the effectiveness of mechanisms to mitigate the agency problems, including boards of directors, shareholders, auditors, lenders, and management compensation.
7. Stakeholder Capitalism and Responsible Business:
• Differentiate between shareholder and stakeholder capitalism.
• Explore the principles of responsible business and their importance in modern corporate financial management.

Key Transferable Skills
At the end of this module students will have developed the following skills:
• Written communication
• Numeracy
• Financial Information processing

Management is a broad field that encompasses a wide range of activities and perspectives. This course focuses on how and why firms differ in what they do and how they perform. We examine how large-scale societal changes shape the conditions under which firms operate, why profitability varies across markets, and how firms develop and position their strategies.

Emphasis is placed on developing an analytical understanding of real-world business phenomena and on linking conceptual perspectives to contemporary developments in the global economy. An international perspective is therefore a recurring element throughout the course.

As indicated in the title, the course is designed as an interactive learning environment in which students actively contribute through short presentations, case discussions, and group work.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students are expected to:

1. Understand the main perspectives used to explain differences in firm strategy and performance.

2. Apply course perspectives in the analysis of concrete cases and engage constructively in discussion with other students.

3. Develop the ability to formulate and communicate their own analytical observations and questions in English, both orally and in writing.

Note that while a certain command of English is necessary, students will not be graded on their vocabulary, grammar or pronunciation. Instead, focus lies on students' abilities to convey their thoughts on the concepts covered throughout the course.

Course Contents:
Lectures introduce the core perspectives of the course: the reasons for international expansion, the configuration of global activities, entry into foreign markets, the internal organization of multinational firms, and the challenges and advantages associated with being foreign. The lectures provide a common conceptual foundation and include interactive elements and discussion.

Case discussions form the core application of perspectives covered in the lectures. There are two different types of case sessions in this course. In the instructor-led case sessions, the analytical approach is demonstrated through guided discussion. In the student-led case sessions, participants develop their own cases based on contemporary business developments or firsthand observations, present them in class, and lead the discussion.

Reaction talks are very short individual presentations. Each student introduces a recent development related to international management and raises a question for class discussion. The purpose is to connect course contents to current events and to stimulate curiosity-driven learning.

This course examines global marketing through the lens of cultural differences and their influence on consumer behavior, market formation, and brand success. It addresses questions such as: Why has Korean popular music achieved global success? Why do people in Japan consume KFC on Christmas? By analyzing such phenomena, students will develop a deeper understanding of how culture shapes markets and consumption practices.

The course introduces key theories and concepts in cross-cultural marketing, including cultural context, symbolic meaning, and the role of intermediaries (e.g., gatekeepers) in market development. Students will learn to apply these frameworks to real-world cases and to critically evaluate global marketing strategies.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:

- Explain major theories and concepts in cross-cultural marketing
- Analyze how cultural differences influence consumer behavior and market outcomes
- Apply theoretical frameworks to interpret global marketing phenomena
- Develop and present a research-based analysis of a cross-cultural marketing case

Course Contents:
Detailed guidance will be provided in the first class; however, the course will generally follow the structure outlined below.

Each class will be divided into two parts. The first half will consist of a lecture based on the textbook, followed by an interactive discussion. Students are expected to actively participate by responding to questions and engaging critically with the material.

The second half of each class will be dedicated to student research projects on global marketing cases across cultures. Students will report on their progress, and their work will be discussed collectively. As a reference for these projects, the instructor will introduce two research streams: the development of the Japanese manga market in the United States and the evolution of Japanese cuisine in the United States.

A midterm presentation will be held as a project debriefing session. Based on the feedback received, students will further refine and develop their research. In the final class, students will present their completed projects. In addition, they will be required to submit a written essay accompanying their presentation.

Student projects are expected to demonstrate the application of course theories to empirical cases, with an emphasis on analytical rigor, conceptual clarity, and the ability to connect cultural context with marketing outcomes.

Students may conduct primary data collection (e.g., surveys, field observations, or interviews) as part of their research projects, where appropriate.

This course examines how and why firms operate across national borders and how international activities reshape strategy and organization. It introduces the main analytical perspectives used to understand international management and applies them to contemporary business developments.

As indicated in the title, the course is conducted as an interactive learning environment. Students actively contribute through short individual presentations, case discussions, and group work. Emphasis is placed on developing an analytical understanding of real-world phenomena and on linking conceptual perspectives to current developments in the global economy.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students are expected to:

1. Understand the main perspectives used to analyze the different parts of international management, including the motives for internationalization, the configuration of global activities, entry strategies, internal organization of multinational firms, and the challenges associated with operating in foreign contexts.

2. Apply these perspectives in the analysis of concrete cases and engage constructively in discussion with other students.

3. Develop the ability to formulate and communicate their own analytical observations and questions in English in a clear and structured way.

Note that while a certain command of English is necessary, students will not be graded on their vocabulary, grammar or pronunciation. Instead, focus lies on students' abilities to convey their thoughts on the concepts covered throughout the course.

Course Contents:
Lectures introduce the core perspectives of the course: the reasons for international expansion, the configuration of global activities, entry into foreign markets, the internal organization of multinational firms, and the challenges and advantages associated with being foreign. The lectures provide a common conceptual foundation and include interactive elements and discussion.

Case discussions form the core application of perspectives covered in the lectures. There are two different types of case sessions in this course. In the instructor-led case sessions, the analytical approach is demonstrated through guided discussion. In the student-led case sessions, participants develop their own cases based on contemporary business developments or firsthand observations, present them in class, and lead the discussion.

Reaction talks are very short individual presentations. Each student introduces a recent development related to international management and raises a question for class discussion. The purpose is to connect course contents to current events and to stimulate curiosity-driven learning.

This course starts from a simple but important question: why do many innovations that appear superior fail to spread? Instead of focusing on the early stages of invention, the course examines what happens when firms try to implement, scale, and gain acceptance for new products and services, particularly across organizational units and national contexts.

The course emphasizes active participation, discussion, and collaborative learning. A central element of the course is a joint group project in which students analyze the dissemination of a specific innovation over the duration of the course. The project is developed through a series of seminars and is complemented by instructor-led and student-led case discussions based on real-world situations.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students are expected to:

1. Understand the main challenges that arise when firms attempt to implement and disseminate innovations within organizations and across markets and countries.

2. Analyze how organizational conditions, market responses, and institutional contexts influence the adoption of new products, services, and practices.

3. Develop and present a cumulative group analysis of a specific innovation, connecting theoretical perspectives to empirical observations.

4. Communicate their ideas and analytical observations clearly in English through presentations, discussions, and written work.

Note that while the course is conducted in English and active participation is expected, students are not graded on vocabulary, grammar, or pronunciation. The focus is on the ability to express and discuss ideas and to use course concepts in an analytical way.

Course Contents:
Lectures introduce the core perspectives used in the course. They focus on the conditions that make the internal scaling and external adoption of innovation difficult, and how firms attempt to overcome those difficulties. The aim of the lectures is to provide a common conceptual framework that students can use in their project work and in the analysis of cases.

A central element of the course is a joint group project in which students analyze the dissemination of a specific innovation. The project is developed step by step through three developmental seminars. In the first seminar, groups define their research focus and analytical approach. In the second seminar, they present their ongoing analysis and receive feedback. The third seminar is devoted to the final presentation of the project.

There are two different types of case sessions in this course. Instructor-led case sessions demonstrate how the analytical perspectives introduced in the lectures can be applied to real-world situations. In the student-led case sessions, small groups are responsible for presenting and leading the discussion of selected cases. These sessions provide an opportunity to compare different innovation challenges and to further develop analytical and communicative skills.

This course develops students’ knowledge of international strategic innovation by examining how organizations reshape the mechanisms through which they create, deliver, and capture value. It introduces a structured multi-level framework that distinguishes innovation in activities and positioning, business models, and broader industry or institutional systems. Through this framework, students acquire analytical and conceptual knowledge enabling them to diagnose competitive environments and identify where innovation can most effectively transform organizational performance. The course explicitly incorporates a global mindset, using international comparisons to demonstrate how innovation strategies are embedded in different institutional, cultural, and economic contexts. Students learn to evaluate the transferability of strategic models across regions and to understand how national systems, regulation, and market structures influence innovation outcomes. This course expectations regarding responsible management education also integrates a social responsibility perspective. It examines how legitimacy, sustainability, and stakeholder expectations shape viable business models and long-term strategic success. Students develop the ability to assess both the economic viability and societal impact of international strategic innovation choices. By combining conceptual frameworks, international case analysis, and applied diagnostic tools, the course supports the development of critical thinking, integrative decision-making, and responsible strategic judgment in a global business environment.

Course Goals:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Demonstrate conceptual knowledge of strategic innovation and explain how it differs from product or technological innovation.
2. Apply a multi-level analytical framework to diagnose innovation opportunities in activities, business models, and broader competitive systems.
3. Analyze how strategy and business models interact, and evaluate how their alignment affects organizational performance and sustainability.
4. Interpret strategic innovation in a global context, recognizing how institutional, cultural, and regulatory environments influence viable strategies across regions.
5. Assess the transferability of innovation strategies internationally, identifying constraints and adaptation requirements.
6. Evaluate the economic, social, and environmental implications of strategic innovation decisions from a responsible management perspective.
7. Integrate stakeholder and legitimacy considerations into the design of business models and strategic choices.
8. Develop evidence-based strategic recommendations that combine competitive advantage, global awareness, and societal responsibility.

Course Contents:
This course is organized around four blocks:
Block 1 - Foundations of Strategic Innovation: Sessions 1–2
What students learn
Students acquire the conceptual foundations of strategic innovation and learn to distinguish between product innovation, strategic positioning, and business model change. They develop the ability to diagnose innovation at multiple levels of analysis and to understand how institutional contexts shape strategic possibilities.
What students do through international cases
Through comparative cases from different regions, students analyze how firms succeed or fail depending on the level at which they innovate. These cases introduce the global perspective of the course and encourage students to consider how strategy and legitimacy vary across markets and institutional environments.

Block 2 - Strategy as the Driver of Economic Architecture: Sessions 3–6
What students learn
Students understand how competitive strategy shapes cost structures, value chains, pricing logic, and long-term profitability. They learn how activity systems, positioning choices, and capabilities determine the economic foundations of a firm’s performance.
What students do through international cases
Students examine firms from different industries and countries to analyze how strategic positioning translates into economic outcomes. International comparisons help them see how competitive advantages are constructed differently across contexts, sectors, and institutional settings.

Block 3 – Innovation in Business Models as Strategic Systems Innovation: Sessions 7–10
What students learn
Students explore how business models can shape competitive behavior, industry dynamics, and organizational priorities. They study subscription, platform, data-driven, and sustainable models to understand how value creation and capture mechanisms influence strategy.
What students do through international cases
Students analyze platform firms, digital companies, and sustainable innovators from multiple regions to understand how business models operate under different regulatory, cultural, and market conditions. Cases highlight how the same model may succeed in one context and fail in another.

Block 4 — Coherent Innovation Proposals or How to Integrate Strategy, Business Models, and Institutions: Sessions 11–14
What students learn
Students develop the ability to integrate strategy, business model logic, and institutional constraints into coherent innovation proposals. They examine transformation processes, regulatory dynamics, scalability challenges, and the role of legitimacy and responsibility in strategic decision-making.
What students do through international cases
Students work with complex international cases and their applied projects to diagnose industries, identify strategic constraints, and design viable innovations. They work on their ability to evaluate international innovation strategies that balance competitiveness, global awareness, and societal impact.

A History of European Economic Integration, 1945-1993

This course provides an introduction to the history of Western European economic integration during the second half of the twentieth century. It covers the period from reconstruction immediately following World War II to the end of the Cold War and the founding of the European Union in the first half of the 1990s.

The course takes a political and global perspective. This means we will focus on how national, international, and supranational politics shaped economic integration. In addition to European actors, we will also discuss the roles that actors from the United States and Japan played in shaping European economic integration in practice.

The course is structured thematically, addressing crucial themes in Western Europe’s economic development. These themes have been selected to reflect both core economic issues—such as market regulation, capital flows, and trade—as well as issues of particular relevance today—such as energy, the environment, and social welfare. This means that we will not simply trace institutional change or the trajectories of quantitative indicators of economic integration and transformation. Rather, we will examine key themes and how the basic decisions regarding their incorporation into European integration were implemented under the influence of economic, political, and social forces.

Structure:
1. Introduction
2. Reconstruction, the Marshall Plan, and the OEEC
3. Integration, Markets, and European and the European Economic Communities
4. Prices, Protection, and the Common Agricultural Policy
5. Competition, Industry, and European Market Governance
6. Multinationals, Local Production, and European Investment Regulation
7. Global Finance, Capital Liberalization, and the OECD
8. Social Harmonization, Worker Protection, and the European Welfare State
9. Global Trade, the Japanese Challenge, and the European Commercial Policy
10. Nuclear Research, Atomic Energy, and EURATOM
11. Oil Shocks, the International Energy Agency, and European Energy Policy
12. Industrial Pollution, Emissions Standards, and European Environmental Policy
13. The Single Market, German Reunification, and the European Union

Course Goals:
The central aims of the course are twofold. The first major aim is to provide students with an understanding of the diversity and complexity of economic decision-making and to highlight the many contingencies facing economic and political actors. The course will trace the variety of institutions, ideas, and terms—many of which were later discarded or relegated to minor roles—that were debated at crucial junctures in the history of European integration, and it will discuss both continuities and ruptures. One corollary of this approach is that we will not focus solely on the central European organizations—i.e., those that would later form the core of the European Union—but also on lesser-known and less well-researched organizations such as the Economic Commission for Europe (ECE), EURATOM, and the OEEC/OECD. The second major aim is to provide students with an understanding of how the European political economy functions at the inter- and supranational levels.

Further aims:
• Understand important economic concepts.
• Acquire basic knowledge of Western Europe’s economic (and political) history.
• Acquire the ability to place economic developments into their historical contexts.

Course Contents:
The course consists of lectures, discussions of important economic terms, short videos, and summaries of the weekly themes (on Thursdays). It is structured thematically, but the themes follow a more or less chronological order based on the periods in which they became significant for the first time.

Industrial Organization is a field of economics that primarily analyzes firm behavior in imperfectly competitive markets. Because it covers a wide range of firm behaviors — including production, pricing, product differentiation, advertising, research and development, entry and exit, and mergers — it is closely related to fields such as Strategic Management and Marketing. It also examines the market outcomes as well as consumer and social welfare that arise from firms' decisions, so it is useful for evaluating various policies such as competition policy and consumer policy. In recent years, the growing availability of data and advances in empirical methods have spurred its practical application to business strategy and public policymaking. The field draws on various analytical tools, such as game theory to theoretically analyze strategic interactions among a small number of firms, and econometrics to empirically test theoretical models using real-world data.

In this course, we study modern empirical industrial organization, which grounds empirical research in rigorous economic theory, detailed data, and in-depth institutional knowledge of specific industries. More specifically, we cover (i) estimation of demand models for differentiated products, (ii) estimation of production functions, and (iii) estimation of static games. If time permits, we cover additional topics such as estimation of auction models, estimation of dynamic games, and selected applied topics.

Course Goals:
The goal of this course is for students to master the basic methods of empirical industrial organization so that they are capable of critically reading prior research. A more ambitious goal is that students are able to develop original research on topics of their own interest using the methods covered in this course.

Course Contents:
This course will cover the following topics.
(i) Introduction (Class #1)
(ii) Estimation of demand functions for differentiated products (Class #2 – Class #5)
(iii) Estimation of production functions (Class #6 – Class #8)
(iv) Estimation of static games (Class #9 – Class #11)
(v) Additional topics (Class #12 – Class #13)
Additional topics may include estimation of auction models, estimation of dynamic games, and selected applications.

Course Overview:

Academic and Professional Presentations I (APP I) is a graduate-level course available to advanced undergraduates that offers students an opportunity to develop skills, language, strategies and experience delivering presentations in English to a general academic audience on an academic topic of interest. The focus is on how to create and deliver presentations that will actively engage an international audience. Equal weight will be given to developing fluent presentation delivery skills and creating interesting, understandable, and memorable content.

APP I is especially appropriate for students in the 1st year of a Masters program or 3rd year of an undergraduate program because the course does not require students to have independent research data or results to report (that is the focus of APP II). For students who do not yet have a completed research plan but who are in the process of reviewing the literature and narrowing down a topic of interest into a feasible research project, APP I can be helpful in presenting and getting feedback on your initial research ideas, leading to a research proposal for the final presentation.

In APP I, students learn the characteristics of an effective academic or professional English language presentation that would be appropriate for an international conference. Competence and confidence is improved not only through repeated practice but also by watching and analyzing model presentations and those of classmates and themselves, giving and receiving structured feedback, and having multiple opportunities to present. In addition to three formal presentations, most days, students will informally present and discuss their presentations with classmates and receive feedback that will help them to improve.

Course Goals:

• Deliver an engaging academic presentation
• Communicate the importance of your research project to a general academic audience
• Present research from the audience’s point of view
• Create a story about your research
• Prioritize key information
• Storyboard a presentation (slides + script)
• Use strategies to maximize the impact of both content and delivery
• Use all 3 presentation channels (verbal, visual, physical)
• Use pathos to present academic information in a truly engaging manner
• Use visuals appropriately
• Manage a Q&A session

Students will assess model presentations according to an evaluation rubric and then create their own presentation script and slides, revising their presentations according to feedback received from their instructor, their classmates and themselves. Special attention will be given to attracting the audience, selecting and organizing content, designing a presentation using Powerpoint, and supporting slide visuals with a script. Presentation delivery will be practiced, and will focus on presence, gestures, intonation, and using the language of spoken academic English. Participants will deliver three presentations to the class, revising each one based on the feedback received from the instructor, classmates and their own self-assessment.

1) Research-based Academic Writing I (RBAW I) is a two-term 13-week course with one meeting per week. Students must take both fall and winter terms.

2) RBAW I must be completed before taking RBAW II. Both courses are offered only in the fall/winter terms. In order to take RBAW II in your final year of study, RBAW I should be taken the previous year.

RBAW I is the first course of a two-course academic writing sequence aimed at helping students report their research in English. The major goal of RBAW I is to develop a cohesive academic paper with a convincing argument based on a strong thesis statement and high-quality and properly cited supporting evidence obtained through library research. We accomplish this through several smaller writing tasks, leading up to a 10-page problem-solution argumentative paper supported by a reference list with at least 10 academic sources.

The course takes a process approach to writing, which means that discussion, critique, analysis, and revision are all important steps in creating a well-crafted academic text. Each task is not written just once but at least two times, with your revisions incorporating the feedback you receive from peers and instructor. Each week, students will develop in class and at home specific elements of their academic English writing, learning its purpose and features, analyzing model texts, taking a critical view of their own writing and that of classmates, and revising the original draft to improve it. As feedback is an important part of the writing and revision process, students will often discuss their own writing and that of classmates in class.

Course Goals:
After completing RBAW I, students will have learned how to:

• write appropriately in academic English, from sentence to paragraph to 10-page paper;
• create an academic argument based on a strong thesis statement;
• work efficiently with ideas by creating an outline of an argument before writing it in paragraphs;
• write a problem/solution argument and know where it appears in academic papers;
• incorporate outside sources into your argument through library research;
• learn “fast reading” techniques to process the research literature efficiently;
• avoid plagiarism by writing well by properly summarizing, quoting and paraphrasing sources;
• properly cite sources both in-text and in a list of references;
• provide an extended definition to increase logical precision and clarify important concepts in your argument;
• incorporate visual data into your argument.

Course Contents:
This course begins with ideas. Students learn to create a strong thesis statement about a topic of interest and then develop that thesis into an outline of an argument. Students then find sources (i.e. research by others, socioeconomic data etc.) that support their argument. The argument is then improved through additional supporting evidence in visual form and extended definitions that clarify important concepts. In developing the final paper, students will create multiple drafts, making revisions based on feedback from classmates and instructor. Finally, the argument is written into a 10-page academic argumentative paper with at least 10 sources in an appropriately formatted references list.

1) Research-based Academic Writing II (RBAW II) is a two-term 13-week course with one meeting per week. Students must take both fall and winter terms.
2) RBAW I must be completed before taking RBAW II. Both courses are offered only in the fall/winter terms. For students in their last year of study, it may be possible to take both RBAW I and RBAW II at the same time with permission of instructor.

RBAW II aims to prepare new scholars to publish an article in an international English-language peer-reviewed journal. Students will complete a research-based paper in English that reports their original empirical or theoretical research either in the IMRD (Introduction, Methods/Model, Results, Discussion) scientific style OR the interpretive style that is common for reporting qualitative research in the social sciences, humanities and law. A journal article for publication has both similarities and differences from a graduation thesis. This course will help you write your graduation thesis, but the final paper for this course is NOT your thesis.

Through homework assignments, class activities and discussion, students will write each section of the paper and then incorporate feedback received to rewrite each section. The course takes a process approach to writing, which means that each writing task is written more than once because discussion, critique, analysis, and revision are all important steps in creating a well-crafted academic text. The course begins with students choosing a research project that they have already completed or almost completed (e.g. a part of their senior undergraduate, MA or PhD thesis) and a target journal for which the research is well-suited.

After reviewing the qualities of a successful journal paper, we perform a genre analysis of a typical article in the student’s target journal to discover the characteristics of a ‘typical’ article in that journal. We then work on writing and rewriting successive sections of the paper, from the title, abstract, introduction and methods/model sections to the discussion and conclusion sections, referring to the published writing in the target journal.

Course Goals:
This course aims to prepare new scholars to publish an article in an international English-language peer-reviewed journal. Students will complete a research-based paper in English that reports their original empirical or theoretical research either in the IMRD (Introduction, Methods/Model, Results, Discussion) scientific style OR the interpretive style that is common for reporting qualitative research in the social sciences.

After completing RBAW II, students will have learned how to:

• Utilize the IMRD (Introduction, Method/Model, Results, Discussion) structure of social science;
• Write each section of an academic paper, including: title, abstract, introduction, literature review, method/model, results, discussion, conclusions;
• Properly incorporate visual elements (figures and tables) and equations into a manuscript;
• Appropriately highlight and hedge claims;
• Strategically use grammar, especially verb tense and word order, to increase cohesion and coherence and to keep it clear to the reader “who did what”;
• Write to the expectations and needs of international English-language editors and reviewers.

Course Contents:
The course takes students step-by-step through the process of writing a research paper in English that reports their original empirical or theoretical research in the IMRD (Introduction, Methods/Model, Results, Discussion) scientific style or the interpretive/qualitative style. Successful writing is iterative, consisting of several drafts with revisions based on the feedback one receives, and we will practice this writing process through class discussion and feedback from peers and instructor. Each week, students at home will read the next topic in the text and write the first draft of that section. Gradually, by the end of the course, you will have a completed paper that has undergone several drafts and revisions of each section.
