International organizations’ activities cover almost every aspect of our lives, encompassing the environment, health, human rights, peace and security, science, transportation, and trade. Because of their pervasive influence, their work, operations, and efficacy are points of discussion. For instance, news articles and commentators scrutinize the Security Council’s failure in stopping war in Gaza and Ukraine, the World Health Organization’s guidelines for responding and preventing the spread of COVID-19, and the impact of the African Union’s membership suspension, such as Sudan’s, in responding to coups and violence. These discussions raise the question: do existing theoretical approaches and frameworks explain the varying behaviours of international organizations?

The objective of this course is to understand existing theories on international organizations and assess their applicability empirically. This course provides an overview of studies on international organizations with a particular emphasis on their behaviour. International organizations are established by states, and their work evolves after creation. Numerous scholars explore whether international organizations have autonomy and power and what their sources are.

For the objective, the course consists of mainly three parts. First, we review existing theoretical frameworks and analyze how they explain the behaviour of international organizations. Second, we delve into the work of certain international organizations, such as those involved in peace and security, human rights, and refugees. We critically assess whether these theoretical frameworks explain the actions of these international organizations. Finally, students form groups and present on international organizations of their choice, applying the relevant theories to their analysis. The course incorporates activities of presentations, discussions, and group work.

Course Goals:
By successfully completing the course, students will be able to
• explain the main theories on international organizations,
• apply these theories to real-world examples,
• collaboratively design and present their case studies, and
• develop their own arguments by listening to the opinions of other participants.

Week 1: Orientation
Week 2: Setting the context – understanding international organizations’ activities

Part I: Theoretical frameworks

Week 3: Overview of studies on international organizations
Week 4: International organizations as outcome and intervening variables

Week 6: International organizations as orchestrators
Week 7: Regional organizations

Part II: Empirical cases & preparation of case studies

Week 8: Refugee
Week 9: Peace & security
Week 10: Corruption
Week 11: Human Rights

Part III: Case study presentation

Week 12: Group presentation
Week 13: Group presentation

What kinds of countries are more likely to go to war against each other? Which type of candidates are more likely to win elections? Why do some countries experience civil wars but not others? Does trade increase inequality? These are the questions you may ask when studying Politics and International Relations. To answer and evaluate these questions, data and statistics have become invaluable tools for social scientists.
This course introduces you to the empirical research process used in political science and other disciplines that use data to answer questions. You will learn how to construct theories and hypotheses, and how to test theories using a variety of statistical techniques, including descriptive analysis, hypothesis testing, correlation, and regression analysis. The course will empower you with the skills and confidence needed to produce your own quantitative analyses. In addition, you will learn critical thinking skills to evaluate claims and assertions by using data. These skills will improve your performance in other classes, strengthen applications to graduate school, and make you valuable to potential employers.
In addition to learning how to perform analyses by hand, you will learn how to employ programming and software to perform these tasks. We will use the R programming language and RStudio software. These are powerful tools to manipulate, analyze, and visualize data. Both are free, so you can easily download them to your personal computers.

No prior experience in statistics or programming required.

Course Goals:
The main goals for the course are:
1. Explain how political scientists use statistical methods to test theories about the political world,
2. Analyze and critically evaluate the use of inferential statistics in applied settings,
3. Think probabilistically about evidence for or against a proposition,
4. Use data visualization and statistical techniques–including measures of central tendency and dispersion, hypothesis testing, linear regression, and logistic regression–to
analyze data and answer questions about the world, both by hand and using R,
5. Interpret the results of statistical analyses to lay audiences, both orally and in writing,
6. Apply these techniques as part of an original study that tests a theory about some
political phenomenon.

1. Research Design and Measurement
2. Introduction to R, Data Collection, and Operationalization
3. Dispersion and Intro. to Probability and Inference
4. Introduction to Data Visualization
5. Confidence Intervals and One-sample Tests
6. Bivariate Hypothesis Testing and Statistical Significance
7. Linear Regression
8. Model Specification and Statistical Control
9. Multicollinearity and Outliers
10. Logistic Regression
11. Extensions of Logistic Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation

The course places primary emphasis on causal inference and the use of R. Therefore, it may not be ideal for students whose sole interest is acquiring substantive knowledge in international relations. However, the methods covered in this course are broadly applicable across the social sciences, including political science and international relations.
The course will be conducted in English and delivered online. As a substantial amount of material will be covered within a single semester, regular preparation and review are essential.

Economic security has emerged as one of the most prominent issues in world politics. After decades of focusing on maximizing the rewards of economic interdependence, policymakers around the globe are now scrambling to establish frameworks for managing its risks. Fortunately, scholars of international relations have been thinking about the intersection of economics, power, and security for a long time. This course seeks to introduce students to that scholarship, and how core theories, concepts, and analytical frameworks from the subfields of international political economy and security studies can be applied to understand the national security consequences arising from economic activity in a wide range of contemporary and historical cases.

Course Goals:
At the end of this course, students will:
• Be able to explain the relationship between different types of economic activity (trade, investment, production, et cetera) and national security in contemporary world politics.
• Be able to explain and apply core concepts and theories from international relations to analyze historical and contemporary cases in which economic activity has had consequences for national security.
• Be able to conduct independent research on and communicate original ideas, analysis, and arguments about economic security issues.
• Have an awareness of major topics, debates and research agendas in the international relations literature that deal with the intersection of economics and security.
• Have an awareness of some of the major actors in the economic security domain, including their core policy frameworks and key case studies of their offensive and defensive use of economic security tools.

Artificial Intelligence Governance: National Strategies, International Initiatives, and the Future of AI Regulation examines one of the most pressing legal and policy challenges of our time: how to govern powerful and rapidly evolving AI technologies in ways that are effective, ethical, and globally coherent.
As AI systems become embedded in critical sectors – from healthcare and transportation to finance, defense, and the justice system – governments and international bodies are racing to develop strategies that address risks, assert sovereignty, and define the rules of the digital era. This course offers a global and national comparative perspective on these efforts, investigating how different jurisdictions (including the U.S., EU, Japan, Singapore, and Canada) are approaching AI regulation, and how multilateral initiatives like the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, the Bletchley Declaration, and the United Nations AI resolution are shaping an emerging international governance architecture.
We will also explore the increasingly influential roles of private actors, technical standard-setters, and civil society in designing rules for AI – often outside traditional legal frameworks.
Designed for students in law, public policy, and interdisciplinary programs, this course emphasizes institutional design, legal interoperability, and the geopolitics of emerging technologies. It invites students to engage critically with real-world governance challenges and to think creatively about what effective, fair, and future-ready AI regulation might look like.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Understand foundational AI technologies and their implications for legal systems, including issues of ethics, liability, privacy, and labor.
2. Analyze and compare national AI strategies and regulatory approaches across leading jurisdictions.
3. Critically evaluate international governance initiatives, including their structure, strengths, and limitations.
4. Assess the challenges and prospects for global regulatory harmonization and transnational cooperation.
5. Identify and apply legal and policy frameworks to real-world case studies involving AI deployment in critical sectors.
6. Develop informed perspectives on the role of law in shaping emerging technologies, with attention to power dynamics, rights-based considerations, and institutional feasibility.

Course Contents:
The course is structured into four thematic modules that move from the global to the national, and from theoretical foundations to applied challenges:
1. Foundations of AI and Legal Contexts
o Introduction to artificial intelligence technologies and their implications for law, society, and governance
o Key legal concerns: algorithmic opacity, bias, accountability, liability, and rights-based critiques
o The role of law in shaping innovation and managing societal risk
2. Geopolitics and International Governance of AI
o Mapping the global power dynamics shaping AI governance
o Overview of multilateral initiatives: the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, the Bletchley Declaration, the OECD AI Principles, and the United Nations AI resolution
o The influence of trade regimes, security alliances, and digital sovereignty on the structure of international AI governance
o The tensions between normative alignment, regulatory fragmentation, and techno-nationalism
3. National Strategies and Regulatory Models
o Comparative study of national AI strategies and legal frameworks in the EU, U.S., Japan, Singapore, Canada, and the UK
o Institutional models: regulatory sandboxes, algorithmic impact assessments, and supervisory authorities
o Legal innovations, enforcement mechanisms, and the role of public-private cooperation
4. AI in Critical Sectors and Future Regulatory Challenges
o Case studies of AI deployment in health, transportation, justice systems, and political processes
o Sector-specific regulatory needs and gaps
o Cross-border risks and the challenge of designing agile, adaptive, and accountable AI regulation
o Scenario-building: What does effective and equitable AI governance look like in 2030?

Regulating Disruptive Technologies: Innovation, Risk, and the Law examines how legal and policy frameworks respond to, shape, and interact with technological change. Emerging technologies have the potential to transform economies, industries, and daily life, offering extraordinary opportunities but also bringing profound risks that can challenge legacy socioeconomic and regulatory models. This course asks a critical question: how can law harness the benefits of innovation while minimizing its harms? The course is not just about learning how to strike a balance between new technologies and the rules that shape them, but about understanding and navigating the multifaceted and dynamic tension between innovation, governance, and society’s welfare.
Students will explore the theoretical foundations of innovation governance, including competing approaches to regulatory intervention and the role of the public interest. Through case studies across diverse domains – such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology, renewable energy, and others – we will investigate what makes certain regulatory strategies succeed while others falter. These examples will highlight the practical realities of governance, showing how regulation can enable progress, stifle innovation, or generate unintended consequences depending on context, process, and design.
The course also takes a comparative perspective, examining how different jurisdictions and sectors adapt – or fail to adapt – to disruptive technologies. Moving beyond the abstract question of “what makes good regulation,” students will build a practical toolkit for identifying and managing the true levers of change. These include corporate accountability, ethical norms, and public participation, alongside modern approaches such as multi-stakeholder processes, agile governance, and cross-border coordination.
Designed for students in law, economics, public policy, and interdisciplinary programs, the course emphasizes the interplay between innovation, regulation, and societal impact. It challenges students to think critically and creatively about designing governance solutions that are forward-looking, adaptable, and resilient – capable of navigating uncertainty while ensuring that technological disruption ultimately serves the public good

Course Goals:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Understand core theories of innovation and regulation – Develop a conceptual grounding in innovation theory, regulatory design, and governance models that address the pace, unpredictability, and socio-legal complexity of technological change.
2. Analyze comparative regulatory approaches – Evaluate how different systems, jurisdictions, and sectors regulate disruptive technologies, comparing fragmented, sector-specific regimes with more unified or interoperable approaches, and identifying the contextual factors that drive these choices.
3. Assess the societal impacts of emerging technologies – Critically examine how disruptive technologies affect economic structures, social norms, human rights, and equitable development.
4. Evaluate governance successes and failures – Draw lessons from real-world case studies to identify why certain regulatory strategies succeed, fail, or produce unintended consequences.
5. Examine governance processes and pathways – Understand how governance processes influence regulatory outcomes, including the effects of regionalism and regulatory fragmentation, incumbency advantages and legacy systems, and emerging tools such as multi-stakeholder approaches and agile governance models.
6. Develop design capabilities for future-ready legal frameworks – Gain a practical toolkit for designing legal and policy solutions that balance innovation incentives with safeguards for public interest, equity, and accountability.
7. Apply cross-sectoral insights – Translate lessons from one technological domain to another, recognizing patterns in governance challenges and opportunities across technology fields.

Course Contents:
Part I – Foundations
• What is technology? Defining key terms, concepts, and typologies.
• What is disruptive technology? Identifying characteristics and historical examples.
• History of technology and society: How technological change has shaped human development, economic structures, governance, and culture.
Part II – Regulating Technology
A. Key Regulatory Questions
• Why do we regulate technology? Economic, societal, cultural, and environmental impacts.
• Where does regulation take place? International, regional, national, and subnational levels.
• Who regulates technology? Legislators, regulators, standard-setting bodies, private actors, and multi-stakeholder institutions.
• When to regulate? Anticipatory vs. reactive approaches.
• What to regulate? Inputs, processes, outputs, effects (e.g., production standards, safety, liability).
• How to regulate? Strong vs. soft regulation; Comprehensive vs. sector-specific approaches; Risk-based, performance-based, and outcome-based models
B. Theoretical Frameworks
• Political economy perspectives: From laissez-faire to state control — theories of market intervention from Friedman, Keynes, Marx, Schumpeter, and contemporary innovation theorists.
• Balancing competing objectives: What are some of the key elements to consider when regulating disruptive tech? Technological development, economic growth, fundamental rights, cultural integrity, and national security.
• Interests at stake: Political, economic, societal, and environmental.
• Micro-level tensions: Incumbents vs. disruptors; domestic vs. foreign innovators; short-term vs. long-term priorities.
C. Modern Governance Approaches
• Corporate governance and self-regulation in fast-moving industries, government intervention in regulation and production
• Agile governance and experimental regulation (e.g., sandboxes)
• Multi-stakeholder governance models and their limitations
• Regulatory interoperability and cross-border coordination
Part III – Case Studies
(Selection may vary to reflect current developments)
• Artificial Intelligence: Governance of AI in critical sectors including autonomous vehicles, judicial applications, and political processes.
• Nuclear Power: Regulating high-risk, dual-use technologies; balancing innovation, energy security, environmental and disaster protection, and weapons technologies.
• Renewable Energy: Governance challenges for grid integration, tax incentives, energy transition, and market design.
• Cellular Agriculture: Food safety, IP issues, trade implications, food security, and ethical debates.
Part IV – Application and Design
• Scenario building: Anticipating governance challenges for emerging technologies.
• Policy design exercises: Developing adaptive, inclusive, and future-ready legal frameworks.
• Integrative project: Students will create governance proposals for disruptive technologies of their choice, incorporating stakeholder mapping, regulatory theory, and comparative insights.

This lecture will introduce the history of the Edo period in English and examine its　characteristics while placing it in a world-historical context. Much time will be devoted　to the interpretation and discussion of historical documents (both textual and visual)

The course titled "International Politics and Data Science" is an academic inquiry into the foundational aspects of international politics with a unique emphasis on experiential analysis through data science. The curriculum is designed to provide students with a fundamental understanding of international political theories while engaging them in practical analysis of political scenarios using data science methodologies. While no prior knowledge of data science is required, a certain level of information literacy is expected to assimilate and interpret data-driven insights effectively.

Course Goals:
1.To cultivate an interest in international politics, setting the stage for understanding its complexity through the lens of Asian case studies involving infrastructure and cultural industries.
2.To illustrate the synergy between data science and international politics as a secondary theme, unfolding progressively to reveal its relevance by the course's conclusion.
3.To provide a contextualized appreciation of international politics in Asia, using tangible examples such as railways and cultural sectors to make the subject matter approachable and engaging.
4.To encourage students to perceive the subtleties of how data science can enhance the study of international politics, thereby fostering an integrated perspective without overwhelming the primary focus on political dynamics.

Technology management theory is a theory centered on technology and R&D management, also known as “innovation management”. In the process of commercializing the results of research and technological development as services and products, introducing them to the market, and making them acceptable to a wide range of customers, strategic management is essential in order to survive fierce competition with various competitors, and technology may play a major role in this process. In this lecture, we will cover the fundamentals of R&D management with examples, and discusses the use of data analysis in technology management.

Course Goals:
The aim of this course unit is to equip students with knowledge and critical skills required to examine and analyse the role technology and innovation play in economic development and in the competitiveness of firms, and the factors involved in effective technology and innovation management. It further aims to provide students with an understanding of the main quantitative methodologies used to measure and understand innovation and to apply these to emerging technologies.

Course Contents:
Indicative course content (order may differ):

DAY 1: WHAT IS INNOVATION AND WHY DOES IT MATTER?
The first two sessions will introduce key concepts and start to explore the relationship between technology, innovation and invention and how they differ. We will discuss which actors (individuals and organisations) are involved in the development and implementation of innovations, and look at a specific innovation case to gain a deeper understanding of the sources of innovation.
DAY 2: R&D FOR INNOVATION AND ITS MEASUREMENT
Research and development (R&D) is at the heart of technological innovation. In the first session we discuss what R&D is, and why, and to what extent, different types of firms engage in R&D. The second session will discuss how we can measure innovation, introducing key science and technology indicators, incl. R&D and patent data. This will be followed by a data group exercise.
DAY 3: DIGITAL INNOVATION
We will learn about digital innovation and what it means for the management of innovation.
Students will start their Group work project.
DAY 4: DYNAMICS OF INNOVATION
Student-led discussions of innovation diffusion and consider a specific innovation case to understand how innovations get adopted.
Students will continue Group work.
DAY 5: MANAGEMENT OF TECHNOLOGY AND INNOVATION
Student-led discussions of topics including Open Innovation, external and internal knowledge and technology sourcing, innovation networks and R&D cooperation.
Students will continue Group work.
DAY 6: CAPSTONE AND RECAP
Group Presentation and Discussion; Innovation Competition.

This course introduces the fundamentals of phonetics. Phonetic knowledge plays an important role in foreign language learning by helping students understand different sound systems and develop accurate pronunciation skills. In the latter half of the course, students will conduct an empirical investigation of their own accent patterns. In addition to examining articulation and engaging in auditory introspection, students will learn basic methods of acoustic analysis. The goal of the course is to develop a scientific perspective on the sounds of language.

Course Goals:
・To acquire the ability to understand and apply the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) in phonetic transcription.
・To conduct empirical investigations of accent patterns in Japanese dialects and analyze the results.
・To work collaboratively in groups and deliver academic presentations.

Course Contents:
This course provides a systematic introduction to the fundamentals of phonetics. Students will first learn about the mechanisms of the speech organs and articulation, and acquire basic knowledge of the classification of segmental sounds (consonants and vowels) as well as the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). The course also examines the distinction between phonetics and phonology, and introduces suprasegmental features such as accent and intonation.
Next, students will learn the basics of acoustic analysis and develop practical skills in observing and analyzing speech data. Using Praat, they will analyze recorded speech data by examining waveforms and fundamental frequency (F0), and learn methods for treating speech as objective data.
In the latter half of the course, students will conduct an investigation of their own accent patterns under the theme “The Accent of One’s Own Speech.” (International students may choose to investigate their native language, their own Japanese, or the Japanese of native speakers.) Working in groups, students will organize their findings and deliver a final presentation based on the collected data.

This course will help students to develop a critical understanding of Japan as a multi-ethnic society, both historically and in the present day. In particular, the course will focus on the societal developments in Japan over the last three decades. By focusing on the experiences of diverse ethnic and immigrant groups in Japan, the course will help students understand the ethnic diversity of Japanese society, which in popular imagination continues to be considered an ethnically “homogeneous society.” This ideology that asserts the Japanese people are a single race/ethnic nation has been criticized by scholars since the 1980s, as being based on a myth of ethnic/national homogeneity (単一民族神話: tanitsu minzoku shinwa). This ideology has had a strong influence on what it means for many people in Japan to be Japanese and has profoundly affected the experiences of ethnic minorities living in post-war Japan. By engaging in the assigned readings and through discussions in class, students are expected to think critically about the contexts of arrival and the backgrounds of various ethnic minorities, their role in the labor market, their efforts in adaptation, and the struggles and challenges that they continue to face in Japanese society. Although, the course seeks to cover a diverse range of ethnic groups and relevant topics, students are also encouraged to explore topics that interest them. Throughout the coursework and in class discussion, I hope that the course will provide students with some inspiration to critically think about ways in which human rights can be protected and social justice can be achieved.

The modern ideals of humanitarianism first emerged in Europe in the nineteenth century and came to exert substantial influence over world politics in the twentieth century. Humanitarianism, a set of ideals for promoting human welfare and upholding human dignity, might be considered as representing a universal value beyond criticism. Yet, in reality, the history of humanitarian ventures involves grave dissensions and power politics over the notion of humanity. This course explores the historical process in which the modern ideals of humanitarianism developed in close entanglement with war, conflict, and colonialism from the Second World War up to the present from global perspectives. Starting with student’s presentation about reading assignments, we will discuss various topics on humanitarian enterprises every class. Lectures and discussion will be done in English.

(3) 近現代の人道主義の歴史に関する主要な論点について独自の視点をもって議論できる

This course explores various “why” questions about English through scientific analysis and comparison with Japanese. Drawing on multiple subfields of linguistics—such as phonetics and phonology, syntax, morphology, semantics, psycholinguistics, and second language acquisition—the course examines English and Japanese from diverse perspectives to develop a systematic understanding of the structure and nature of human language.

Rather than emphasizing memorization, the course prioritizes analytical thinking. Students will be trained to examine linguistic data, formulate hypotheses, and test their validity. Through this process, they will develop the ability to approach language from a theoretical and evidence-based perspective.

The course begins with foundational concepts and progresses step by step; therefore, no prior knowledge of linguistics is required.

(1) Classify English vowels based on tongue position and explain their articulation. Additionally, accurately distinguish and produce each vowel sound.
(2) Describe English consonants in terms of manner of articulation, place of articulation, and voicing. Additionally, accurately distinguish and produce each consonant sound.
(3) Correctly pronounce English phonetic symbols and transcribe words you can accurately pronounce using phonetic symbols.
(4) Identify sound changes in English by analyzing written text and explain how sounds transform in different contexts. Additionally, reproduce these phonological changes accurately in speech.
(5) Represent the syntactic structure of English sentences using tree diagrams and explain similarities and differences between English and Japanese through structural comparison.
(6) Analyze given linguistic or experimental data, formulate hypotheses, and evaluate their validity based on evidence.
(7) Distinguish between more effective and less effective methods of second language learning and explain the theoretical reasons underlying these differences.

Why is the basic word order of English Subject–Verb–Object? Why is the past tense suffix -ed pronounced as /t/ in some words and /d/ in others? Why does American English water sound like “wara”? Why do we need to consciously study numerous grammar rules when learning English as a foreign language, whereas we acquire our first language naturally without explicit instruction? Is studying English grammar truly indispensable for becoming proficient in English?

This course explores such “why” questions about English through scientific analysis and systematic comparison with Japanese. Drawing on multiple subfields of linguistics—including phonetics and phonology, syntax, morphology, semantics, psycholinguistics, and second language acquisition—the course aims to deepen students’ understanding of the structure and nature of human language.

Rather than emphasizing memorization, the course prioritizes analytical thinking. Students will examine linguistic data, identify patterns, formulate hypotheses, and test their validity. The goal is to develop an evidence-based and theoretically grounded approach to language analysis rather than relying solely on intuition or experience.

By comparing English and Japanese, students will examine not only differences but also structural similarities between the two languages. Through careful engagement with course materials and assignments, students are expected to gain new perspectives and recognize that English and Japanese share deeper structural principles than may initially appear.

The course also covers foundational concepts in English phonetics and phonology, with the aim of improving practical pronunciation skills. By comparing the sound systems of English and Japanese, students will systematically learn how English vowels and consonants are articulated and develop the ability to produce them accurately. Through analysis of differences between the two languages, students will deepen their theoretical understanding of sound patterns and phonological principles in English.

The course begins with foundational material and proceeds step by step; therefore, no prior knowledge of linguistics is required. In addition to lectures, students will engage in data analysis, problem-solving activities, and group work. Active participation is expected.

♦︎ Modernity in Crisis: Europe since 1914 ♦︎

Language of Instruction: English

This course explores the troubled history of Europe from 1914 to the present day. Beginning with the First World War, the course traces Europe’s trajectory through the Russian Revolution and the rise of fascism, the devastation of the Second World War, postwar economic reconstruction and social change, and the transition to neoliberalism in the late twentieth century, culminating in the myriad challenges that continue to shape Europe today. Beyond core themes of politics, economics, and war, it also examines empire and decolonisation, mass society and popular culture, and the enduring tensions between nationalism and multiculturalism.

The course frames the trajectory of the twentieth century around the idea of ‘modernity in crisis’. Much of the century was defined by ideological conflict between competing visions of modernity rooted in liberalism, communism, and fascism. Each claimed to offer a universal model of social organisation, grounded in strong states, economic management, and scientific expertise. Confidence in such universalist projects, however, weakened after the 1970s as state-managed prosperity gave way to economic crises and instability. Societies once organised around mass political mobilisation, standardised institutions, and shared expectations shifted towards what many intellectuals described as ‘postmodernity’, as identities and lifestyles became more fragmented and individualised.

This is a university-level history course designed for non-history majors, and it is taught entirely in English, with English-language readings, audiovisual materials, and group activities. It prioritises analysis over descriptive coverage, focusing less on ‘what happened’ and more on why it happened, what it meant to people at the time, and how it fits into broader historical narratives. Rather than a textbook-style survey centred on memorising descriptive detail, it foregrounds competing historical interpretations and theoretical explanations, with each lecture organised around a central argument.

Course Goals:
・This course provides a foundational understanding of the key political, economic, social, and cultural changes in modern and contemporary Europe. Students will move beyond basic chronologies by tracing the broader trajectory of the twentieth century through a detailed study of major historical turning points. Assessment is based on participation in small-group activities, short reaction papers submitted after each session, and a final exam.

・Students will develop the ability to construct argument-driven historical interpretations grounded in appropriate historical examples, further deepening their understanding of the course material. These skills will be assessed through group discussions, reaction papers, and a final exam in which students write an argument-driven essay on one of the course’s central themes.

・For non-native English speakers, the course offers an opportunity to engage with European history in an entirely English environment. Through the course’s assessed components, students will improve comprehension of both abstract concepts and concrete historical case studies, and develop the ability to communicate arguments effectively in both speech and writing. The goal is that students can articulate their ideas clearly in an international academic context.

Course Contents:
The course combines lectures with small-group activities. Before each lecture, students are required to complete the assigned readings and audiovisual material. All preparatory materials are compulsory, and both lectures and small-group activities assume that students have completed them.

During the lecture, students will divide into small groups of two to four to discuss questions on the lecture topic and complete source analysis activities. Each group will record their findings in a shared Google Drive spreadsheet distributed via Google Classroom. This process helps students organise their thoughts, articulate their ideas, and contribute useful content that will aid both themselves and their peers in deepening their understanding of the material and revising for the final exam. The tutor will provide feedback after each discussion session and offer opportunities for groups to share their responses with the class.

Students are also required to complete an online reaction paper in English after each lecture, due by the end of the day. Each paper includes a small number of questions that prompt students to reflect on the lecture material and develop their own interpretations. The reaction papers also provide a space for students to ask questions and give feedback on the course content.

This course introduces perspectives on language. We will try to find out how things like sounds and words and meanings and grammar correlate in individual languages and look for things that differ in the languages participants know. By doing that we will get a pretty good overview on what language is. Of course, we need to think about how we can describe those things and - more importantly - why structures developed the way they did. We will see that language change follows patterns.
We will keep things simple because this course essentially is about asking scientific questions: It is a course intended to introduce you to scientific thinking in general.

Course Goals:
In this science yes/no-answers are rare. Therefore, you will have the opportunity to practice discussing topics in a scientific context in a language that is (most likely) not your native one. It also will provide you with an overview on language-related sciences because in many cases scientists from other disciplines found the answers to essential language-related questions.

Course Contents:
This course intends to introduce the wide range of topics linguists are concerned about. We will start with very fundamental questions and assumptions about the nature of language itself and proceed by analyzing basic linguistic structures of those languages participants of this course know. We will soon find out that comparison of languages leads us to linguistic categories some consider universal, which again leads us to interesting questions: If we all have this capacity, why is it so hard to learn a foreign language, for instance. Sometimes not linguistics but psychology or even anthropology gives us clues, thus, we will be looking at some of the findings the science of language owes to other sciences.

This course introduces perspectives on language usage. We will try to find out how we actually do things with language. A question, for instance, may not be intended to be a question but maybe a request or even an insult, we may use deviant speech and by doing so we may express far more than the literal meaning of the sentences we utter and so on. How do we describe those things and - more importantly how do we understand intentions or meanings behind utterances? We will find out how linguists deal with those problems and - in general terms - how language relates to extra-linguistic characteristics of individuals.

Course Goals:
This course is supposed to introduce you to scientific thinking in general using something that is familiar to all of us: language and its usage. It is not easy to find the right questions or even explanations for all the strange phenomena we may encounter when looking closely at the the way we actually use language but we will try without getting too deep into linguistic description. Nevertheless, we will be touching all kinds of human sciences looking for answers and you will have the opportunity to practice discussing topics in a scientific context in a language that is (most likely) not your native one.

Course Contents:
In principle, this course continues the introduction to general linguists of last term but the focus shifts from description of language and its components to language usage. Therefore, students who did not join this class in the first term will not be disadvantaged here - general and applied linguistics are very different in nature. Individual, social and cultural and cognitive aspects of language usage and language learning are the keywords here but we will also take a look at literature and ask ourselves what exactly turns words or sentences into pieces of art.

An Introduction to 20th-Century Poetry Written in Chinese and Japanese (A)

Students and scholars of literature written in a linguistic and cultural background different from their own often focus on the works of a specific time period and/or by a specific group of writers and unfortunately tend to fail to acquire general knowledge of literature written in the target language. This course aims to complement highly departmentalised courses in Chinese and Japanese literature by introducing the works by some of the best-known 20th-century poets writing in Chinese or Japanese primarily to students from outside Chinese- or Japanese-speaking cultures majoring in East Asian studies. Some lines from these poems have entered either of the East Asian languages; a few of the poems have also been set to music. In class, we will also be discussing biographical elements of the poets and the historical contexts in which they composed their poems.
This term, we will also be looking at some song lyrics written by Japanese singer-songwriters contemporary with Bob Dylan, 2016 Nobel laureate for literature, as well as the works of a few ethnically Mongolian or Tibetan poets writing in Chinese and/or Japanese.
Students who do not major in East Asian studies and/or who come from a Chinese- or Japanese-speaking cultural background are also welcome to take the course.
Each week, we will read the featured poems and translate them in part or in full into English. Some knowledge of Japanese and/or Chinese would be of great use, but is not a prerequisite for taking this course. (That said, please keep in mind that that the overall Japanese/Chinese proficiency levels of a particular group might affect the classroom dynamics.) Sufficient knowledge of English to produce readable translations of the poems will be necessary, although the translations need be neither completely accurate nor highly literary.

Course Goals:
To acquire some general knowledge of some of the best-known 20th-century poets writing in Chinese/Japanese and their works; to become familiar with some of the traditional Chinese and Japanese poetic forms; to practise intensive reading of poetic texts through translation.

Course Contents:
Each class will be structured as follows:
- The instructor will provide students with handouts of featured poems two weeks beforehand and explain the words and phrases used in the poems.The students are expected to translate the texts in part or in full into English at home.
- In class, the students will be asked to share some of the above-mentioned translations with their classmates (with a smaller class) or submit their translations beforehand on Manaba (with a larger class).
- The presenter(s) or the instructor will give an analysis of the featured poems with biographical, contextual, and intertextual notes.
- The rest of the class will ask questions about, and/or make comments on, the featured poems.

Course Description

This Course explores the transformative role of diversity in organizations and its implications for future workplaces. This course examines the historical evolution, current trends, and future directions of diversity in organizational contexts, focusing on the dynamics of DEI.

Through foundational theories in organizational behavior, social psychology, and human resource management, students will gain a deep understanding of diversity as a multi-dimensional concept that encompasses gender, race, ethnicity, age, ability, sexuality, and more. Key topics include the evolution of diversity initiatives, the impact of diverse teams on innovation and decision-making, the challenges of managing a diverse workforce, and the critical role of leadership in fostering an inclusive environment.

By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the analytical tools to assess diversity and inclusion strategies and apply evidence-based practices to support fair and productive organizational cultures. Through literature studies, interactive discussions, and real-world applications, students will develop actionable insights into how diversity can be leveraged to drive both ethical and strategic organizational success.

Students can acquire not only knowledge but also perspectives with global mindset and social responsibility through this course.

Course Goals:
The course will be entirely in English. The methodology will combine lecture, literature study, case discussion, personal reflection and exercises. You are expected to participate actively in class.

This course examines how and why firms operate across national borders and how international activities reshape strategy and organization. It introduces the main analytical perspectives used to understand international management and applies them to contemporary business developments.

As indicated in the title, the course is conducted as an interactive learning environment. Students actively contribute through short individual presentations, case discussions, and group work. Emphasis is placed on developing an analytical understanding of real-world phenomena and on linking conceptual perspectives to current developments in the global economy.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students are expected to:

1. Understand the main perspectives used to analyze the different parts of international management, including the motives for internationalization, the configuration of global activities, entry strategies, internal organization of multinational firms, and the challenges associated with operating in foreign contexts.

2. Apply these perspectives in the analysis of concrete cases and engage constructively in discussion with other students.

3. Develop the ability to formulate and communicate their own analytical observations and questions in English in a clear and structured way.

Note that while a certain command of English is necessary, students will not be graded on their vocabulary, grammar or pronunciation. Instead, focus lies on students' abilities to convey their thoughts on the concepts covered throughout the course.

Course Contents:
Lectures introduce the core perspectives of the course: the reasons for international expansion, the configuration of global activities, entry into foreign markets, the internal organization of multinational firms, and the challenges and advantages associated with being foreign. The lectures provide a common conceptual foundation and include interactive elements and discussion.

Case discussions form the core application of perspectives covered in the lectures. There are two different types of case sessions in this course. In the instructor-led case sessions, the analytical approach is demonstrated through guided discussion. In the student-led case sessions, participants develop their own cases based on contemporary business developments or firsthand observations, present them in class, and lead the discussion.

Reaction talks are very short individual presentations. Each student introduces a recent development related to international management and raises a question for class discussion. The purpose is to connect course contents to current events and to stimulate curiosity-driven learning.

4. Enhance critical thinking in assessing risks such as greenwashing, reputational vulnerability, and regulatory change.
5. Enable students to design evidence-based, sustainability-driven marketing strategies that balance competitive advantage with long-term societal value.

♦︎ The Global History of Alcohol: Consumption, Regulation, and Power ♦︎

【Language of Instruction】English (lectures, main course materials); bilingual in English/Japanese where appropriate (small group activities, supplementary course materials, Q&A sessions)

This course explores the global history of alcohol and the politics surrounding it as a ‘problematic’ commodity, one whose regulation and public image have long reflected deeper tensions over morality, governance, public health, and social order. Rather than treating alcohol as just another consumer good, the course approaches it as a complex and contradictory substance that defies simple market logic and continually challenges the boundaries of acceptable consumption. Widely celebrated and enjoyed in some contexts, yet condemned, restricted, or prohibited in others, alcohol offers a unique angle on the development of modern capitalism, the expansion of state power, innovations in marketing and business, the entanglement of science and morality in policymaking, and shifting public attitudes towards vice.

Drawing on case studies from Britain, North America, Continental Europe, and Japan, the course investigates how alcohol has been marketed as a source of pleasure, critiqued by moral reformers and scientific experts, and managed by governments as both a health risk and a source of revenue. It places emphasis on how businesses and industries navigate contested consumer markets and adapt to evolving cultural and policy environments. Students are also encouraged to move beyond the assumption that consumption is purely rational or economic, and instead to understand it as a culturally embedded practice shaped by moral values, social norms, and ideological frameworks. This perspective fosters the ability to critically and contextually reassess contemporary challenges in marketing, branding, public relations, and business ethics.

Course Goals:
・Develop the ability to analyse markets and consumption as products of cultural, political, and social forces by integrating interdisciplinary perspectives from history, sociology, and cultural studies

・Critically assess the limits of Rational Choice Theory (RCT), and use alternative frameworks such as Consumer Culture Theory (CCT) to understand consumption as a culturally embedded practice shaped by moral values, social norms, and ideologies

・Trace how alcohol has been embraced as an object of desire while also becoming a target of social anxiety and, over time, an object of medical and public health governance

・Use historical case studies to examine how states, businesses, consumers, and activists have shaped contested markets, especially where public health, profit, and ethics come into conflict

・Understand the moral dilemmas that come from marketing morally ambiguous commodities, and assess how businesses have responded to shifting social values, public scrutiny, and regulatory change

・Learn to critically read academic texts beyond your own discipline, and apply the gained insights to real-world challenges in marketing, business ethics, and policy

・This course is designated for the assessment of the Competency Goal ‘M(CM)1 (Knowledge)’. Develop the ability to comprehensively understand the central claims or purposes of academic literature, and to review existing literature in a critical manner

Course Contents:
The course is taught primarily in English and combines lectures with small group activities (discussion questions, analysis of primary sources, etc.). Before each class, students must complete the assigned readings, and will also be provided with video materials designed to support a more visual understanding of the lecture content. All preparatory materials are compulsory, and both the lecture and group work proceed on the assumption that students have completed them.

During the lecture, students will be divided into small groups of 2 to 3 and given time to discuss a set of questions on the lecture topic and work on source analysis activities. While students are encouraged to engage in discussions in English to the best of their ability, bilingual discussions will be allowed when necessary to prioritise comprehension of complex class material over language demonstration. Each group will record their discussion in a shared Google Drive spreadsheet distributed via Google Classroom. This process helps students organise their thoughts, articulate their discussions, and contribute useful content that will aid both themselves and their classmates in revising and preparing for the final exam while also deepening their understanding of the material. The tutor will provide oral comments and feedback after each discussion session and facilitate opportunities for students to share their responses with the class.

This course develops rigorous theoretical and applied foundations of econometric analysis at the graduate (Master’s) level. It begins with a review of probability and statistics, emphasizing sampling theory and asymptotic properties of estimators. The course then examines linear regression models with one and multiple regressors, including formal derivation of OLS. Statistical inference is studied through hypothesis testing and confidence intervals. Issues of endogeneity and causal identification are addressed using instrumental variables methods. The course also covers binary dependent variable models estimated by maximum likelihood and panel data techniques that control for unobserved heterogeneity through fixed and random effects. Empirical implementation using R software is integrated throughout to develop independent research skills. The lecture is conducted in English; however, students may submit deliverables in either English or Japanese.

Course Goals:
The objective of this course is to develop a foundational understanding of econometric theory and to enable students to apply it to empirical analysis. Specifically, the course covers probability and statistics, simple linear regression, multiple linear regression, hypothesis testing and confidence intervals, nonlinear regression analysis, instrumental variables methods, and panel data analysis. In addition to acquiring theoretical knowledge, students are expected to gain the ability to conduct basic empirical analyses using real economic data.

International organizations’ activities cover almost every aspect of our lives, encompassing the environment, health, human rights, peace and security, science, transportation, and trade. Because of their pervasive influence, their work, operations, and efficacy are points of discussion. For instance, news articles and commentators scrutinize the Security Council’s failure in stopping war in Gaza and Ukraine, the World Health Organization’s guidelines for responding and preventing the spread of COVID-19, and the impact of the African Union’s membership suspension, such as Sudan’s, in responding to coups and violence. These discussions raise the question: do existing theoretical approaches and frameworks explain the varying behaviours of international organizations?

The objective of this course is to understand existing theories on international organizations and assess their applicability empirically. This course provides an overview of studies on international organizations with a particular emphasis on their behaviour. International organizations are established by states, and their work evolves after creation. Numerous scholars explore whether international organizations have autonomy and power and what their sources are.

For the objective, the course consists of mainly three parts. First, we review existing theoretical frameworks and analyze how they explain the behaviour of international organizations. Second, we delve into the work of certain international organizations, such as those involved in peace and security, human rights, and refugees. We critically assess whether these theoretical frameworks explain the actions of these international organizations. Finally, students form groups and present on international organizations of their choice, applying the relevant theories to their analysis. The course incorporates activities of presentations, discussions, and group work.

Course Goals:
By successfully completing the course, students will be able to
• explain the main theories on international organizations,
• apply these theories to real-world examples,
• collaboratively design and present their case studies, and
• develop their own arguments by listening to the opinions of other participants.

Course Contents:
The course consists of the following topics:

Week 1: Orientation
Week 2: Setting the context – understanding international organizations’ activities

Part I: Theoretical frameworks

Week 3: Overview of studies on international organizations
Week 4: International organizations as outcome and intervening variables
Week 5: International organizations as autonomous actors
Week 6: International organizations as orchestrators
Week 7: Regional organizations

Part II: Empirical cases & preparation of case studies

Week 8: Refugee
Week 9: Peace & security
Week 10: Corruption
Week 11: Human Rights

Part III: Case study presentation

Week 12: Group presentation
Week 13: Group presentation

This course, "EU Research Skills I," is the foundational component of a seminar series designed to enhance students' proficiency in conducting rigorous social science research within the context of European studies. The primary objective is to develop and refine fundamental research techniques, fostering critical thinking and effective communication. Through interactive discussions and collaborative activities, students will apply academic research concepts to their own projects and engage in peer-to-peer feedback in English. Additionally, the course will explore emerging AI research tools and their appropriate, ethical application in academic research.

Course Goals:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

Articulate and Discuss: Present and discuss their research ideas, relevant readings, and research plans with peers in a structured academic setting.

Critical Evaluation: Critically evaluate and effectively communicate key research findings and scholarly works within their specific field of study.

Effective Communication: Practice and refine their ability to communicate research ideas and findings clearly and persuasively in English.

Peer Feedback: Provide and receive constructive feedback on research progress and methodologies.

AI Research Literacy: Critically evaluate AI tools for academic research, apply them ethically and transparently, and integrate AI assistance while maintaining scholarly rigor and originality.

Course Contents:
This seminar will utilize a participatory and collaborative approach. Students will engage in weekly activities directly related to their individual research projects and plans. Key components include:

Weekly Research Reports: Students will submit concise weekly reports detailing their research progress, challenges, and insights.

Peer Review and Discussion: Students will actively participate in peer review sessions, providing constructive feedback and engaging in critical discussions of their peers' research.

Methodological Exploration: Discussions will focus on various social science research methodologies, including data collection, analysis, and interpretation, particularly as they relate to European studies.
English Language Development: The course will provide opportunities to enhance academic English communication skills through presentations and discussions.

AI Research Skills Workshop: Students will explore, evaluate, and share AI research tools (semantic search engines, citation managers, research assistants). Through hands-on sessions, students will practice effective prompting strategies, discuss appropriate use cases versus traditional methods, examine bias and limitations, and develop transparent practices for integrating AI assistance in their research workflows. Each student will present one AI tool to peers and contribute to developing class guidelines for ethical AI usage in academic work.

This is the second part of the seminar EU Research Skills. The course builds on the activities conducted during the first semester and its main aim is to assist the student in writing up his/her graduate research project (e.g. research paper or thesis). Students will also briefly share experiences with research tools, including AI assistance, as they complete their work.

Course Goals:
Throughout the course students are encouraged to apply research methodology concepts to their own studies and share their work with other seminar members. Students will also practice transparent documentation of their research process, including any AI tools used.

1. the techniques for integrated management in the EU
2. the fields and sectors of action of the EU in administering various spaces

Artificial Intelligence Governance: National Strategies, International Initiatives, and the Future of AI Regulation examines one of the most pressing legal and policy challenges of our time: how to govern powerful and rapidly evolving AI technologies in ways that are effective, ethical, and globally coherent.
As AI systems become embedded in critical sectors – from healthcare and transportation to finance, defense, and the justice system – governments and international bodies are racing to develop strategies that address risks, assert sovereignty, and define the rules of the digital era. This course offers a global and national comparative perspective on these efforts, investigating how different jurisdictions (including the U.S., EU, Japan, Singapore, and Canada) are approaching AI regulation, and how multilateral initiatives like the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, the Bletchley Declaration, and the United Nations AI resolution are shaping an emerging international governance architecture.
We will also explore the increasingly influential roles of private actors, technical standard-setters, and civil society in designing rules for AI – often outside traditional legal frameworks.
Designed for students in law, public policy, and interdisciplinary programs, this course emphasizes institutional design, legal interoperability, and the geopolitics of emerging technologies. It invites students to engage critically with real-world governance challenges and to think creatively about what effective, fair, and future-ready AI regulation might look like.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
1. Understand foundational AI technologies and their implications for legal systems, including issues of ethics, liability, privacy, and labor.
2. Analyze and compare national AI strategies and regulatory approaches across leading jurisdictions.
3. Critically evaluate international governance initiatives, including their structure, strengths, and limitations.
4. Assess the challenges and prospects for global regulatory harmonization and transnational cooperation.
5. Identify and apply legal and policy frameworks to real-world case studies involving AI deployment in critical sectors.
6. Develop informed perspectives on the role of law in shaping emerging technologies, with attention to power dynamics, rights-based considerations, and institutional feasibility.

Course Contents:
The course is structured into four thematic modules that move from the global to the national, and from theoretical foundations to applied challenges:
1. Foundations of AI and Legal Contexts
o Introduction to artificial intelligence technologies and their implications for law, society, and governance
o Key legal concerns: algorithmic opacity, bias, accountability, liability, and rights-based critiques
o The role of law in shaping innovation and managing societal risk
2. Geopolitics and International Governance of AI
o Mapping the global power dynamics shaping AI governance
o Overview of multilateral initiatives: the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, the Bletchley Declaration, the OECD AI Principles, and the United Nations AI resolution
o The influence of trade regimes, security alliances, and digital sovereignty on the structure of international AI governance
o The tensions between normative alignment, regulatory fragmentation, and techno-nationalism
3. National Strategies and Regulatory Models
o Comparative study of national AI strategies and legal frameworks in the EU, U.S., Japan, Singapore, Canada, and the UK
o Institutional models: regulatory sandboxes, algorithmic impact assessments, and supervisory authorities
o Legal innovations, enforcement mechanisms, and the role of public-private cooperation
4. AI in Critical Sectors and Future Regulatory Challenges
o Case studies of AI deployment in health, transportation, justice systems, and political processes
o Sector-specific regulatory needs and gaps
o Cross-border risks and the challenge of designing agile, adaptive, and accountable AI regulation
o Scenario-building: What does effective and equitable AI governance look like in 2030?

Regulating Disruptive Technologies: Innovation, Risk, and the Law examines how legal and policy frameworks respond to, shape, and interact with technological change. Emerging technologies have the potential to transform economies, industries, and daily life, offering extraordinary opportunities but also bringing profound risks that can challenge legacy socioeconomic and regulatory models. This course asks a critical question: how can law harness the benefits of innovation while minimizing its harms? The course is not just about learning how to strike a balance between new technologies and the rules that shape them, but about understanding and navigating the multifaceted and dynamic tension between innovation, governance, and society’s welfare.
Students will explore the theoretical foundations of innovation governance, including competing approaches to regulatory intervention and the role of the public interest. Through case studies across diverse domains – such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology, renewable energy, and others – we will investigate what makes certain regulatory strategies succeed while others falter. These examples will highlight the practical realities of governance, showing how regulation can enable progress, stifle innovation, or generate unintended consequences depending on context, process, and design.
The course also takes a comparative perspective, examining how different jurisdictions and sectors adapt – or fail to adapt – to disruptive technologies. Moving beyond the abstract question of “what makes good regulation,” students will build a practical toolkit for identifying and managing the true levers of change. These include corporate accountability, ethical norms, and public participation, alongside modern approaches such as multi-stakeholder processes, agile governance, and cross-border coordination.
Designed for students in law, economics, public policy, and interdisciplinary programs, the course emphasizes the interplay between innovation, regulation, and societal impact. It challenges students to think critically and creatively about designing governance solutions that are forward-looking, adaptable, and resilient – capable of navigating uncertainty while ensuring that technological disruption ultimately serves the public good

Course Goals:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Understand core theories of innovation and regulation – Develop a conceptual grounding in innovation theory, regulatory design, and governance models that address the pace, unpredictability, and socio-legal complexity of technological change.
2. Analyze comparative regulatory approaches – Evaluate how different systems, jurisdictions, and sectors regulate disruptive technologies, comparing fragmented, sector-specific regimes with more unified or interoperable approaches, and identifying the contextual factors that drive these choices.
3. Assess the societal impacts of emerging technologies – Critically examine how disruptive technologies affect economic structures, social norms, human rights, and equitable development.
4. Evaluate governance successes and failures – Draw lessons from real-world case studies to identify why certain regulatory strategies succeed, fail, or produce unintended consequences.
5. Examine governance processes and pathways – Understand how governance processes influence regulatory outcomes, including the effects of regionalism and regulatory fragmentation, incumbency advantages and legacy systems, and emerging tools such as multi-stakeholder approaches and agile governance models.
6. Develop design capabilities for future-ready legal frameworks – Gain a practical toolkit for designing legal and policy solutions that balance innovation incentives with safeguards for public interest, equity, and accountability.
7. Apply cross-sectoral insights – Translate lessons from one technological domain to another, recognizing patterns in governance challenges and opportunities across technology fields.

Course Contents:
Part I – Foundations
• What is technology? Defining key terms, concepts, and typologies.
• What is disruptive technology? Identifying characteristics and historical examples.
• History of technology and society: How technological change has shaped human development, economic structures, governance, and culture.
Part II – Regulating Technology
A. Key Regulatory Questions
• Why do we regulate technology? Economic, societal, cultural, and environmental impacts.
• Where does regulation take place? International, regional, national, and subnational levels.
• Who regulates technology? Legislators, regulators, standard-setting bodies, private actors, and multi-stakeholder institutions.
• When to regulate? Anticipatory vs. reactive approaches.
• What to regulate? Inputs, processes, outputs, effects (e.g., production standards, safety, liability).
• How to regulate? Strong vs. soft regulation; Comprehensive vs. sector-specific approaches; Risk-based, performance-based, and outcome-based models
B. Theoretical Frameworks
• Political economy perspectives: From laissez-faire to state control — theories of market intervention from Friedman, Keynes, Marx, Schumpeter, and contemporary innovation theorists.
• Balancing competing objectives: What are some of the key elements to consider when regulating disruptive tech? Technological development, economic growth, fundamental rights, cultural integrity, and national security.
• Interests at stake: Political, economic, societal, and environmental.
• Micro-level tensions: Incumbents vs. disruptors; domestic vs. foreign innovators; short-term vs. long-term priorities.
C. Modern Governance Approaches
• Corporate governance and self-regulation in fast-moving industries, government intervention in regulation and production
• Agile governance and experimental regulation (e.g., sandboxes)
• Multi-stakeholder governance models and their limitations
• Regulatory interoperability and cross-border coordination
Part III – Case Studies
(Selection may vary to reflect current developments)
• Artificial Intelligence: Governance of AI in critical sectors including autonomous vehicles, judicial applications, and political processes.
• Nuclear Power: Regulating high-risk, dual-use technologies; balancing innovation, energy security, environmental and disaster protection, and weapons technologies.
• Renewable Energy: Governance challenges for grid integration, tax incentives, energy transition, and market design.
• Cellular Agriculture: Food safety, IP issues, trade implications, food security, and ethical debates.
Part IV – Application and Design
• Scenario building: Anticipating governance challenges for emerging technologies.
• Policy design exercises: Developing adaptive, inclusive, and future-ready legal frameworks.
• Integrative project: Students will create governance proposals for disruptive technologies of their choice, incorporating stakeholder mapping, regulatory theory, and comparative insights.

After the lectures, students discuss questions posed by the instructors in order to consolidate their knowledge. In the second half of the course, depending on the number of students enrolled, there will be about seven lectures in which students will give presentations on court cases in international law. - Understanding the basic structure of the international community and international law;
- Identifying international community interests;
- Identifying main ideas and problems;

This course explores the field of International Relations from a non-conventional standpoint. More precisely, it employs research methodologies of gender and sexuality studies and uses them to approach/ analyze IR issues.

While some understanding of gender/ sexuality might be helpful, curiosity and open-mindedness would be far more valuable. I intend this course to be a seminar-type course. There will be a lot of discussion, where we exchange different ideas. As a matter of fact, the discussion has been central since this course was first introduced several years ago, and hopefully, it remains that way, whether online or in person. I respect your personal thoughts and feelings.

Course Goals:
“The Personal is Political” is one of the well-known feminist slogans from the 1970s, and I would like to take this up as a course policy; while theories and textbooks are important, let us become closer to the subject. Hopefully, at the semester's end, you will have "felt" how gender works in the international arena.

Because every thought counts, I do not tolerate any attitude that is indifferent or judgmental. If you cannot appreciate differences, PLEASE DO NOT SIGN UP FOR THIS COURSE.

The readings will be selected based on everyone's interests. I will be posting reading possibilities later.

If you are uncomfortable speaking publicly, you can write down your thoughts. You can share them via Manaba or "chat" at the beginning of the session.

Session 14: Review.

The Japanese government has extended international cooperation for the past 70 years. It has revised its ODA Charter in June 2023, along with the direction to address global issues through bilateral and multilateral cooperation, as well as through agenda-setting and rulemaking in the international arena. This course exposes students to Japanese policies towards a wide range of global issues and foreign relations, by inviting front line practitioners and analysts as guest lecturers to share their experience in dealing with the global and regional issues. Students are to be requested to actively engage in analyzing issues of their interest to develop their own critical thinking.

Course Goals:
This course aims to enhance students’ understanding on Japan’s foreign policy in the context of global governance. The course is held in collaboration with JICA, Japan International Cooperation Agency, under its Development Studies Program launched in 2018. Learning from Japan’s experience since the second world war, the course was first held in 2018 elaborating on why and how international cooperation would be needed for sound development of developing countries. Ever since, many issues have been revisited, considering newly emerging challenges such as climate change and pandemic. Student notably from the developing countries, and from post-conflict, or from post-natural disaster countries, could draw good lessons from Japan’s experiences when they return home and take part in their nation building.

Course Contents:
Japan’s international cooperation is to be analyzed with practical perspectives being provided by former Ambassadors and professionals in the government, experts from JICA, international organizations, NGOs and the media. The course will shed a light on nexus between Japan’s Foreign Policy and International Development with a particular focus on conflict areas such as Gaza and West Bank, Syria, Iraq, Sudan, Ukraine, Mindanao and others. Through highlighting these conflict areas, appropriate contemporary topics such as human security, global health, peace and security, refugees and IDPs will be further discussed. This year the course will focus on more political issues in the changing world order. The students are requested to actively participate in the deliberation through such means as choosing a topic of their interest and introducing issues and wrapping-up the discussions.

This class tackles with the most fundamental question regarding the state; how do states survive and promote their interests in an "anarchical" international society. It deals with war, nuclear deterrence, conflict resolution, and other emerging security issues.
