This course (conducted in English) introduces the principles and tools used to design, conduct, and evaluate empirical research in International Relations. It focuses on presenting the students with core methods and techniques used in the discipline, as well as the philosophical and theoretical background of methods to conduct research in the field.

The objective of the class is to help students apply the contents to their own research designs, whether it is for their thesis, a particular class, or their professional development. In other words, the emphasis is not only on understanding methods, but on their applicability.

To achieve this, the course is divided into three core parts. First, introductory and theoretical lectures on research questions and theory building, to causal inference approaches, qualitative and quantitative logics, and scientific reasoning. Students will be challenged with questions such as “what does a proper research puzzle look like?” and “how do methods prove causality between dependent and independent variables?”. As discussion, students are encouraged to understand the strengths and weaknesses of qualitative methods for IR research.

Secondly, we will explore different qualitative and mixed methods commonly used in IR research. Case studies (and their selection criteria), process tracing, text and content analysis, fieldwork and archival research, interviews and focus groups, and finally surveys and experiments. Each of these method reviews is accompanied with a practical example. The class introduces a selection of methods, but students are free to research and apply any framework for research in International Relations. In the discussion, students will be required to assess whether a method is proper to answer a research problem.

Thirdly, we will focus on research practical considerations, limitations, and ethical considerations for conducting research. Students are encouraged to present their own research proposal or methodological assessment. The course is expected to be an open debate and to close with an in-class discussion of the use of AI in research, its impact on ethics, methods, and research in general.

CLASS STRUCTORE: The first part of each class is a theoretical presentation of the contents, and the second part is a discussion based on the readings and the examples. Not all the readings used for the class are mandatory. Mandatory readings will be explicitly highlighted by the professor before the class.

Course Goals:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
(1) Understand the importance of a proper methodological design in the conduction of academic research projects;
(2) Formulate their own clear, researchable questions and theoretical arguments;
(3) Select and critically assess qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods appropriate to a research question;
(4) justify decisions about case selection, measurement, and data collection;
(5) design research that takes ethics, transparency, and reproducibility seriously; and
(6) present a coherent research prospectus in written and oral form.

What kinds of countries are more likely to go to war against each other? Which type of candidates are more likely to win elections? Why do some countries experience civil wars but not others? Does trade increase inequality? These are the questions you may ask when studying Politics and International Relations. To answer and evaluate these questions, data and statistics have become invaluable tools for social scientists.
This course introduces you to the empirical research process used in political science and other disciplines that use data to answer questions. You will learn how to construct theories and hypotheses, and how to test theories using a variety of statistical techniques, including descriptive analysis, hypothesis testing, correlation, and regression analysis. The course will empower you with the skills and confidence needed to produce your own quantitative analyses. In addition, you will learn critical thinking skills to evaluate claims and assertions by using data. These skills will improve your performance in other classes, strengthen applications to graduate school, and make you valuable to potential employers.
In addition to learning how to perform analyses by hand, you will learn how to employ programming and software to perform these tasks. We will use the R programming language and RStudio software. These are powerful tools to manipulate, analyze, and visualize data. Both are free, so you can easily download them to your personal computers.

No prior experience in statistics or programming required.

Course Goals:
The main goals for the course are:
1. Explain how political scientists use statistical methods to test theories about the political world,
2. Analyze and critically evaluate the use of inferential statistics in applied settings,
3. Think probabilistically about evidence for or against a proposition,

This course introduces the foundations of causal inference and the use of the statistical software R, both of which form the basis of quantitative analysis in the social sciences. The course places particular emphasis on practical application.

Course Goals:
The goals of this course are as follows:
- To understand the basics of causal inference.
- To acquire a working knowledge of R for data analysis.
- To understand applications in the social sciences, particularly in political science and political economy.

Course Contents:
The first five sessions focus on the fundamentals of programming in R. No prior programming experience is required; however, these sessions will be relatively technical. They provide essential foundations for conducting data analysis.
The course then turns to the basic methods of causal inference (e.g., instrumental variable, regression discontinuity design, and difference-in-differences). In each session, I will give a lecuture, followed by hands-on exercises in R to help students learn quantitative methods in practice.
The course places primary emphasis on causal inference and the use of R. Therefore, it may not be ideal for students whose sole interest is acquiring substantive knowledge in international relations. However, the methods covered in this course are broadly applicable across the social sciences, including political science and international relations.
The course will be conducted in English and delivered online. As a substantial amount of material will be covered within a single semester, regular preparation and review are essential.

【Overall theme】
Re-interpretation of Asian Economic Development: Development State vs Autonomous Economic Agents

【Main topics】
I. Why are some countries rich while others remain poor?
- The relationship between economy and democracy
II. How did the West achieve its economic development?
-. City: Learning lessons from the urban commercial centers of Italy and the Netherlands.
- The Corporation: A key institutional driver behind Britain's Industrial Revolution.
-. Individuals and Knowledge: The U.S. as a “European dream” for a free society and innovation.
III. How could Asia catch up with the West?
- Japan: The first Asian nation to successfully implement Westernization and industrialization.
- Korea: Benchmarking Japan’s Westernization while shifting its model toward the U.S.
- China: Standing at a crossroad between continued economic expansion and political reform
IV. Perspective on the future Asian economic development

Course Goals:
【Goals】
Asia has been steadily narrowing the gap with the West. Just as Japan developed its economy by rigorously adopting Western systems, South Korea followed a similar path—though the underlying causes of this growth are often overlooked by Koreans themselves. While China is also catching up, its growth is decelerating too rapidly for it to become a dominant global power. This raises the question: Can Asia truly overtake the West? Answering this requires a historical and comparative analysis of the long-term relationship between economic and political development. Against this backdrop, this course concludes that there is no unique 'Asian model'; rather, Asian success stems not from specific Asian values, but from the liberal values learned from the West. Specifically, this course re-examines the rise of the West and Asia’s subsequent convergence to draw critical lessons for the future of the Asian economy.

Economic security has emerged as one of the most prominent issues in world politics. After decades of focusing on maximizing the rewards of economic interdependence, policymakers around the globe are now scrambling to establish frameworks for managing its risks. Fortunately, scholars of international relations have been thinking about the intersection of economics, power, and security for a long time. This course seeks to introduce students to that scholarship, and how core theories, concepts, and analytical frameworks from the subfields of international political economy and security studies can be applied to understand the national security consequences arising from economic activity in a wide range of contemporary and historical cases.

Course Goals:
At the end of this course, students will:
• Be able to explain the relationship between different types of economic activity (trade, investment, production, et cetera) and national security in contemporary world politics.
• Be able to explain and apply core concepts and theories from international relations to analyze historical and contemporary cases in which economic activity has had consequences for national security.
• Be able to conduct independent research on and communicate original ideas, analysis, and arguments about economic security issues.
• Have an awareness of major topics, debates and research agendas in the international relations literature that deal with the intersection of economics and security.
• Have an awareness of some of the major actors in the economic security domain, including their core policy frameworks and key case studies of their offensive and defensive use of economic security tools.

Subtitle: Cross-cultural Understanding

Conditions
This course offers face-to-face classes only (No online class delivery will be provided). Information contained in the course syllabus may be subject to change with advance notice, as deemed appropriate by the instructor in charge of the course.

Course Description:
This course is conducted entirely in English and is designed to equip students with a paradigm—a mental model—for living and communicating with people from cultures other than his/her own. As the environmental context for this course, Japan and Japanese culture will be discussed extensively throughout the semester. The course will begin with an examination of culture—what constitutes national culture, and how it is reflected in the way people communicate. Then we will examine in-depth one approach to analyzing culture—Geert Hofstede’s five dimensions—and, using those dimensions, identify behavioral markers among the cultures from which students come, draw conclusions about the differing cultures, and investigate how to communicate effectively with people from different cultural backgrounds. This course will also examine other cultural concerns, including shame and guilt cultures, Uchi and Soto, intercultural communication, micro-cultures within broader cultural contexts, and, finally, the impact of stereotyping on our communication behavior.
Moreover, the issues addressed in this course include, but are not limited to, verbal and nonverbal norms, the rules and etiquette of communication across cultures, culture shock, negotiation, multicultural teamwork, leadership and decision-making, and ethical issues in intercultural communication.
The course comprises a good mixture of lectures, class discussions, and workshops. Only serious students are asked to attend.

Course Goals:
Course Objectives:
The goal of this course is to both acquire intercultural communication skills and enhance mutual understanding of cultural diversity in today’s global society by providing diverse perspectives on culture and communication. By the end of the semester, students should be able to:

1. Describe Hofstede’s dimensions of culture, giving illustrations of extreme positions in each dimension
2. Identify the position of your own culture along the Hofstede continua
3. Identify behavioral markers of Hofstede’s dimensions in other cultures and how each would impact your own communication behavior
4. Describe alternative approaches to the study of cross-cultural communication and points of commonality among them
5. Understand the major practical issues of cross-cultural communication
6. Acquire an intermediate level of competence in managing and resolving problems and issues with counterparts from other cultures

Subtitle: Japanese Business Culture

Conditions
In principle, this course offers only face-to-face classes, except for makeup classes.
Information contained in the course syllabus may be subject to change with advance notice, as deemed appropriate by the instructor in charge of the course.

Course Description:
This course is conducted entirely in English and is designed to assist students who seek to bring cross-cultural theory and research into their business practices in order to develop the intercultural competence necessary to interact confidently and successfully with Japanese businesspeople. To achieve these goals, this course includes both theoretical discussions and intercultural sensitivity workshops. The comparative approach will allow us to examine how people practice business differently, depending on explicit and implicit sets of general cultural assumptions, rules, norms, and values. We will work hard to understand cultural differences in business people’s attitudes towards work, companies, and the relationship between individuals (colleagues or co-workers and clients/customers) and organizations (counterparts or partners). We will also try to understand the possible cultural roots of Japanese business practices and behavior, and turn our attention to phenomena that are only indirectly observable, such as harmony, loyalty, discipline, patience, respect for senior staff, and the importance of moderation.
This course consists of four sections. First, we will review Hofstede’s five dimensions of culture and related cultural concepts in order to learn how to analyze cultural differences at the national level. Second, the basic cultural concepts and orientations that underpin Japanese business customs will be explored. Third, the characteristics of Japanese corporate culture will be presented and discussed in light of the differences from one’s own culture. Fourth, this course will offer practically oriented workshops to illuminate key cultural differences.
This course comprises a good mixture of lectures, class discussions, and workshops. Only serious students are asked to attend.

Course Goals:
Course Objectives:
Upon completion of this course, students will (1) be familiar with the unique characteristics of Japanese organizations and management practices from a comparative perspective, (2) be able to identify cultural variables affecting Japanese people at work, and (3) have an increased awareness of the dynamics in Japanese business environments and culture.

* Understand the key issues and policies of the Japanese labor market in the context of globalization and an aging population in Japan.
* Comprehend Japanese corporate culture, the Japanese approach to human resource management, and current trends in diversity management aimed at retaining talented individuals.
* Critically analyze gender issues in the workplace in Japan.

This course provides students with theoretical and practical knowledge of the role and impact of global marketing & new product development (NPD) on business activities in Japan.

The main objectives of this course in marketing are:
・ To learn the principles and key concepts of global marketing
・ To deepen the understanding of the uniqueness and commonality of Japan in a global market.
・ To explore approaches to designing and implementing global marketing strategies for Japan, emphasizing the impact of environmental factors.

For the new product development part, students are expected:
・ To understand the new product development (NPD) process and its principles for success in the Japanese market.
・ To learn how to transform consumer insights into prototypes and launch products in Japan successfully.
・ To enhance their analytical and intercultural communication skills to effectively exchange ideas and insights for new product opportunities in Japan.

Course Goals:

6. Understand situations and challenges that new product developments (NPD) encounter and demonstrate solutions to manage such situations through case studies.

This lecture attempts to show the way to "Smart Shrink". So what is that "Smart Shrink"? That is, as a response to population decline, we do not try to stop the population decline by force, but aim for a society in which the well-being of the people is maintained and improved even under the face of population decline. Currently, the Japanese economy is in the midst of a population decline problem, but population decline is not a problem unique to Japan. It is assumed that countries around the world will also face the problem of population decline sooner or later. By studying the Japanese economy facing population decline ahead of other countries and learning lessons from it, students will develop knowledge and ideas that will be useful to Japan and other countries facing population decline in the future.

Course Goals:
The goal of this lecture is to help students learn about the Japanese economy facing the problem of population decline and solving its difficulties, and to acquire a way of thinking about the problem of population decline, which will become a global problem in the future. The knowledge gained from this lecture will surely be useful when each student's home country faces demographic problems in the near future. 　Specifically, we will grasp the actual situation of the population decline problem facing the Japanese economy. And learn that it is not a problem limited to Japan. In particular, I understand that Asian countries are following Japan's population decline problem. In response to the problem of population decline, students will recognize the difficulty of recovering the population, and learn the importance of changing social and economic systems that can adapt to population decline on the premise that the population will decline. In order to solve the problem of population decline, it is necessary to take into account the characteristics of each country and coordinate various interests such as urban and rural areas, generations, and genders. The goal of this course is to enable students to recognize the issues that students will be able to cope with future population problems in their home countries and to explore solutions based on them.

Course Contents:
A total of 13 lectures are planned. The contents of each lecture are as follows.
Lecture 1: "Introduction and Basic Knowledge of Japanese Finance"
In the first lecture, you will introduce the faculty, explain future class developments, grade evaluations, and office hours. After that, he explains the state of Japanese finances.

Lecture 2: "Population decline is an inevitable trend"
In the second lecture, we will learn that Japan's population decline is inevitable for the time being.

Lecture 3: "Looking at the World Population"
The third lecture deals with the future of global population flows. It shows that not only Japan, but also the population of the world as a whole is declining.

Lecture 4: "Well-being and Economic Challenges in the Context of Population Decline"
In the fourth lecture, it is shown that the population onus is the biggest background to economic issues. After that, we will discuss the relationship between population size and people's well-being, growth policy under population decline, and economic policy.

Lecture 5 & 6: "Responding to Labor Shortages"
In the fifth and sixth lectures, we will discuss how to respond to the labor shortage, which has been rapidly progressing in recent years. The population decline that is the premise of Smart Shrink is not that each age group is declining evenly, but that the working-age population (15~64 years old) is decreasing, which leads to a labor shortage. The keyword that appears here is "Lewisian Turning Point".

Lecture 7 & 8: "Business Management under Population Decline"
In the seventh and eighth lectures, in an economy with a declining population, in the job market, firms become weaker as buyers, and employers become stronger as sellers. This indicates that it is necessary to reform the personnel system of Japanese companies. By analyzing companies that are popular with new graduates, we explore the conditions for companies that are selected by students.

Lectures 9 & 10: "How to Maintain the Sustainability of Social Security"
The ninth and tenth lectures cover social security issues such as pensions, medical care, and nursing care. Japan's social security system basically adopts a system in which current workers support the elderly. This method is no longer sustainable under the population onus. In this context, we will explore the issues to maintain the sustainability of the social security system. In particular, we will consider how to reduce the waste of medical expenses.

Lecture 11: "Smart Shrink in the Region"
In the 11th lecture, we will consider how regions should coexist with population decline. Looking ahead to future population changes in the region, the population decline is particularly significant in rural areas. In this sense, the rural area is at the forefront of Smart Shrink.

Lecture 12: "Population Decline and Climate Change"
In the 12th lecture, we will address the issue of climate change under a declining population. Decarbonization in climate change countermeasures is a major global trend, and Japan needs to take further action. Population decline is positive for carbonization because it reduces greenhouse gas emissions from human activities. However, the impact of disaster relief through population decline is not very large. It is explained that Japan needs to further strengthen its efforts to address climate change issues in the future.

Lecture 13: "Summary"
In the 13th lecture, we will review the contents of the lectures so far and try to consolidate knowledge through questions and answers. In addition, explain about the final exam.

This course is composed of a history section that looks back on the history of the Japanese economy since the end of the war and explains the path it has taken up to the present, and a section that analyzes the current state of the Japanese economy theoretically and objectively and explains the challenges it faces.

The history section of the Japanese economy, which consists of the first half of the 13 lectures, explains the Japanese economy chronologically, with themes including high economic growth, the end of high economic growth and maturation, the emergence of the bubble, the collapse of the bubble and economic stagnation, the impact of the global financial crisis (Lehman Shock), and Abenomics. In doing so, objective explanations are provided using data, graphs, and tables. For this reason, the class also explains the definitions of data and how to read graphs and tables. Elements of the international economy are also incorporated throughout. The global economy surrounding the Japanese economy is also covered, including comparisons with major countries and relationships with the international economy.

In the second half of the lecture, which is divided into individual topics, the current Japanese economy will be analyzed from various perspectives, such as globalization, trade and international balance of payments, labor markets, low birthrate and aging population and social security, fiscal policy, monetary policy, and financial systems. This approach will clarify the issues facing the Japanese economy. In doing so, data, graphs, and tables from reports by the Bank of Japan and white papers published by government agencies will be introduced, and students will learn how to interpret them and understand their implications.

Through the first and second halves of the lecture, students are expected to acquire and solidify systematic knowledge about the Japanese economy by understanding the Japanese economy from both a chronological and cross-sectional perspective. It is also expected to be useful in acquiring policies and ideas aimed at solving the issues facing the Japanese economy. It is also expected that the use of data, graphs, and tables will lead to the acquisition of logical expression and thinking methods.

Course Goals:
The goal of this course is for students to acquire basic knowledge about the history of the postwar Japanese economy and the modern Japanese economy, and to be able to form their own thoughts and opinions about the issues facing the Japanese economy and the direction the Japanese economy should take to overcome these issues.

Specifically, students are expected to acquire the following four main abilities: 1) To be able to understand the "Outlook Report" published by the Bank of Japan, the government's monthly economic report, and various white papers. 2) To be able to not only understand technical terms, but also to interpret the meaning of data, graphs, and tables and explain them themselves. 3) To be able to access databases provided by the government and the Bank of Japan, obtain the necessary data, process it according to the purpose of analysis, and finally create graphs and tables. 4) To be able to understand the causes of the issues facing the Japanese economy, form their own ideas about the policies and directions to resolve these issues, and be able to explain them persuasively to others.

Furthermore, students are expected to participate enthusiastically in classes and understand the historical significance of Japan's postwar economic development and the international importance of the current Japanese economy. The main goal of this course is for students to understand the impact that the high economic growth of the postwar Japanese economy had on the world and Asian economies, and to understand its historical significance. It is also important for students to understand the role and significance of the globalized Japanese economy in the current international economy. It would be my pleasure if students come to understand that overcoming the challenges that will be explained in this course will be beneficial not only for Japan, but for the world as well.

Course Contents:
A total of 13 lectures are scheduled. The contents of each lecture are as follows.
1st lecture: Introduction and basic knowledge of macroeconomic analysis
In the first lecture, the instructor will be introduced, future course developments, grading, office hours will be explained, and basic knowledge of macroeconomic analysis that will be useful for understanding the lectures will be explained.

2nd lecture: Source of high economic growth
In the second lecture, the source of Japan's high economic growth will be explained through explanations of growth accounting, changes in industrial structure, household savings rate, demographic bonus, and nuclearization of families.

3rd lecture: End of high economic growth and maturation of the economy
In the third lecture, the end of high economic growth and maturation of the economy will be explained through explanations of the yen revaluation, dollar shock (Nixon shock), theory of remodeling the Japanese archipelago, oil crisis, hyperinflation, and excess liquidity.

4th lecture: Emergence of the bubble
In the fourth lecture, the emergence of the bubble will be explained through explanations of Reaganomics, Japan-US trade friction, stock prices and land prices, capital gains, and the Plaza Accord.

5th lecture: The bubble collapse and economic stagnation
In the 5th lecture, the collapse of the bubble and economic stagnation will be explained through explanations of stock price declines, the collapse of the land myth, balance sheet adjustments, deflation, three excesses, and financial system instability.

6th lecture: From the global financial crisis to Abenomics
In the 6th lecture, the impact of the global financial crisis on the Japanese economy and the subsequent Abenomics (three arrows, new three arrows, unconventional monetary policy, high stock prices and a weak yen, public debt) will be explained.

7th lecture: Globalization and changes in industrial structure
In the 7th lecture, the globalization of the economy and changes in industrial structure will be explained through explanations of corporate activities, changes in industrial structure, direct investment, overseas sales ratios, supply chains, and changes in Japanese companies.

8th lecture: Trade and balance of payments
In the 8th lecture, trade and balance of payments will be explained through explanations of comparative advantage, opportunity cost, primary income balance, external asset balance, EPAs and FTAs, etc.

9th lecture: Labor market
In the 9th lecture, the labor market will be explained through explanations of the productive age population, labor force, employed persons, self-employed persons, labor shortages, and the ratio of women in managerial positions.

10th lecture: Low birthrate and aging population and social security
In the 10th lecture, low birthrate and aging population and social security will be explained through explanations of the total fertility rate, average life expectancy, population onus, social security benefits, pay-as-you-go system, and macroeconomic slide.

11th lecture: Fiscal policy and fiscal circumstances
In the 11th lecture, fiscal policy and fiscal circumstances will be explained through explanations of the function of finance, the effects of fiscal policy, fiscal rigidity, primary balance, and fiscal dominance.

12th lecture: Role and evolution of monetary policy
In the 12th lecture, the role and evolution of monetary policy will be explained through explanations of central banks, monetary policy meetings, unconventional monetary policy, inflation targeting, Quantitative and Qualitative Monetary Easing (QQE), negative interest rates, etc.

13th lecture: Evaluation of the financial system
In the 13th lecture, the financial system and its evaluation will be explained through explanations of the Financial Services Agency, the deposit insurance system, macro-prudential policy, the financial system report, macro stress testing, etc.

Journalism and the Power of the Press in Japan asks you to think about and discuss the principle of press freedom through its expression here in Japan. Over the course, you will delve into the Japanese free press' sometimes troubled history and present reality, while grappling with questions that go to the heart of not just journalism, but to definitions of the "public good" and the health of democratic systems. For example: Is state control of the news media ever justified? Looking at real-world situations for context, your own responses to that question may surprise you.

Course Goals:
Using historical and present-day case studies, you will examine what press freedom means in practice, and the different ways it can be restricted. For example, does keeping secrets and imposing penalties for reporting them count as limiting press freedom? You will do this by:
- examining the early days of print news in Japan, and the dark days of the descent into war;
- discussing types of information control, and present-day law and attitudes to secrecy;
- questioning, through real-world examples, whether there are any ethical limits to freedom of the press and expression;
- comparing coverage of the same issues in different publications;
- an approx. 2,000-word formal essay on a question related to press freedom or freedom of speech;
- team debates on those same questions;
- and talking about how news is covered from day to day, through class analysis of at least one real-time news article per week (of your choosing).

1: What is journalism for?
Outline of the course. Reflections on your assumptions about the purposes of journalism. Class discussion. ★Short essay assigned.★
2: Small Paper, Big Paper, Huge Paper
Introducing Japanese print news outlets and reporting styles. Comparison with English-language newspapers.
3: Censorship and Self-censorship I
A little bit of history on the early days of Japan's news business -- and information control -- starting in the Meiji period. Class discussion.
★Short essay due★
4: War and the News
Delving into the treacherous space between news and propaganda in WWII Japan. What is the news media's responsibility during wartime?
★Debate groups formed, midterm essay assigned★
5: Censorship and Self-censorship II
Flash forward to Japan’s present. What should and should not be a secret? Is freedom of speech under threat in Japan?
6: Access Journalism

Subtitle: Finance, Sustainability, and System Change

This course treats finance as a mechanism that drives the real economy and society, covering topics ranging from the structure of traditional finance to ESG, climate risk, Japan's GX (Green Transformation) strategy, and carbon pricing. Through the lens of capital allocation and policy formation, students will examine the conditions under which finance can have a positive impact on social systems.

Course Goals:
1. Explain how finance influences social decision-making.
2. Compare the roles of banks and non-bank financial institutions, and of public and private markets.
3. Analyze ESG factors and climate risk from the perspective of corporate value.
4. Explain Japan's GX strategy and the institutional design challenges it entails.
5. Produce written reports and deliver presentations in English.

Course Contents:
This course views finance not merely as a collection of financial products or technical skills, but as a system that shapes decision-making in the real economy and society through capital allocation, risk-sharing, price formation, information, and incentives.

In the first half of the course, students will study the evolution of financial markets and compare the roles of banks, non-banks, public markets, and private markets to understand the achievements and limitations of traditional finance. Building on this foundation, the course distinguishes between sustainable investment and sustainable finance, examining ESG, materiality, climate risk, disclosure, stewardship, and transition finance from the perspectives of both investor decision-making and financial system design.

The latter part of the course focuses on Japan's GX (Green Transformation) strategy, carbon pricing, and the GX ETS, tracing the pathways through which institutional rules lead to real-world outcomes through corporate behavior and capital allocation. Ultimately, students will explore the conditions under which finance can maximize its positive impact on economic, environmental, and social systems through capital allocation, engagement, collaboration, and policy formation.

Throughout the term, a combination of lectures, case studies, discussions, and a group project (Final Project Paper) will enable students to develop the ability to conduct evidence-based analysis and provide professional proposals in English.

FAKE / NEWS: Can you tell the difference? And what is "fake news" anyway? Come to think of it, what is "news"?
This course asks you to step back from the torrent of information we all live in and take a hard look at these questions. Along the way, we will address how major news organizations present information, and how purveyors of disinformation do the same.

Course Goals:
We will delve into how information about our world is fed to you online, and how it is used to manipulate you (yes, YOU) for commercial and political ends. And, if we agree this is a problem, we will tackle who is responsible for cracking it. Lastly, we will ask where journalism stands in all this. Is good journalism a shield against mis- and disinformation, or does it help it spread? Is it even the journalists' problem?

Course Contents:
1: Introduction
Let's start with a very basic question: What is news, and what is "fake news"?
★Short assignment set★
2: News and Democracy
Conventional wisdom has it that a well-informed public, and thus journalism, is essential to a healthy democracy. Is this true?
★Short assignment due★
3: News and Bias
How does bias manifest in news articles?
★Presentation groups formed, midterm essay assigned★
4: Narrative Power
How news narratives shape opinion on the issues of the day. And how resistant these narratives are to change even when new facts emerge.
5. Propaganda
What is it? How is it done? Is it that different today than it was in the pre-online world?
6: Mis-/Disinformation
What's the difference? How do you build a disinformation article? And why do it?
7: FEAR + ANGER
8: Filter Bubbles, Echo Chambers, and Algorithmic Information Shaping
Do online filter bubbles and echo chambers exist? How do algorithms affect what we see on social media, and on news sites?
★★Midterm papers due★★
9: How much do you know? (I mean, really?)
Discovering our own ignorance, and biases that shift our thinking.
10: Film discussion
Let's talk about, and critique, The Great Hack.
11: It's all Meta's fault!
Is it social media firms' responsibility to combat fake news and online opinion manipulation?
12: It's all mainstream media's fault! Journalism in the fake news era.
Are professional journalists and news outlets responsible for fanning the fake news flames? And what can journalists or news organisations do to push back the disinformation tide? Where do we all go from here?
13: Group presentations.
14. Group presentations.

本授業では、日常生活を中心としたテーマからアカデミックジャパニーズの基礎的な内容までを扱いながら、中級前レベルの日本語運用能力を４技能（聞く・話す・読む・書く）で総合的に伸ばします。自己紹介、依頼、予約、相談、誘い、苦情など、実際の場面を想定したコミュニケーション活動に取り組むとともに、日本の文化を知る多様な文章を読み、内容理解と情報の取り出しを行います。また、手紙や説明文などの短い文章を書く練習を通して、表現力を高めます。

This course is for students who have mastered hiragana and katakana, approximately 150 kanji characters, and the first half of beginner-level grammar. The course is designed to develop practical skills in the four skills of reading, writing, listening, and speaking Japanese. The class will provide many exercises based on situations that students will encounter in their daily lives, aiming to enable students to communicate in Japanese outside of class.

Course Goals:
Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:
1. Listening： understand simple conversations on topics related to daily life;
2. Speaking： communicate in everyday situations in Japanese and make short presentations in Japanese.
3. Reading： read short texts in hiragana, katakana, and about 195 kanji characters.
4. Writing： write short passages using hiragana, katakana, and kanji characters.

Course Contents:
This course develops high‑beginner Japanese skills in listening, speaking, reading, and writing, with a focus on daily life. Students will practice everyday communication and work with short texts, including about kanji.

※Please refer to the “Class Schedule Details” for the overall course schedule. A detailed daily schedule will be distributed in class.

Course Goals:
The aim of this course is to bridge the gap between knowledge and performance to allow students to reach the intermediate level. This course requires prior knowledge of Hiragana, Katakana, and approximately 150 Kanji.

Course Contents:
・Vocabulary Building: Expand vocabulary knowledge and practical usage related to university life and daily activities.
・Point Listening: Identify key details in fast-paced Japanese conversations.
・Non-stop speaking: Practice keeping the dialogue moving and sustain interactions with others.
・Peer-reading: Read Japanese texts and engage in collaborative discussions to share diverse opinions.
・Kanji and writing: Master Kanji essential for daily life and apply them in essay writing.
・Presentation: Design and deliver formal oral presentations entirely in Japanese.

※The schedule is subject to change.

Japan experienced a steady economic growth since Meiji era started; but, she now faces many challenges such as population aging, low fertility, poverty, regional disparities and low economic growth. In order to have a good understanding of the transformation of the Japanese economy, we review success and failure of Japanese fiscal and monetary policies in Japan and try to find reasons for them.

Course Goals:
There are two goals of this course. The first goal is to have good understandings of Japan's fiscal and monetary policy making. The other goal for students is to be able to apply what they learned in the course to consider fiscal and monetary policies in the countries they are interested in (e.g., their home countries).

Course Contents:
We will have ten lectures on the following five topics (two lectures for each topic) concerning Japan's Fiscal and Monetary Policy Making. The following schedule of the lectures is tentative and the order of five topics may be changed slightly. The final schedule will announced in the first lecture.

Lecture 1, 2: A Brief History of Japan's Economy and Society (Prof. Yamashige)
Lecture 3, 4: Fiscal Policy Making: Fiscal System and Intergovernmental Relation (Prof. Sato)
Lecture 5, 6: Fiscal Policy Making: Social Security System (Prof. Yamashige)
Lecture 7, 8: Fiscal Policy Making: Tax System (Prof. Yamashige)
Lecture 9, 10: Monetary Policy Making: Financial System and Monetary Policies (Prof. Sekine)
Lecture 11, 12, 13: Student's Short Presentation and Discussion

In the last three classes we will have students' presentation of their small research on some fiscal and/or monetary policies, including the process of their historical development, in countries of their interests (e.g., home countries). The presentation can be seen as a proposal of the final report (in about 2,000 words). The final report is expected to be a kind of application of what students learned in the lectures, and will be evaluated from such viewpoints.
